content.title: Adult Essential Hypertension Screening and Confirmation

redFlags: Severe elevation with chest pain, dyspnoea, neurological deficit, confusion, visual loss, or acute kidney injury
Pregnancy with elevated pressure or pre-eclampsia symptoms
Abrupt onset, resistant readings, or suspected secondary cause
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic
Occasional non-specific headache or dizziness, which cannot establish diagnosis
physicalSigns: Elevated pressure on correctly performed measurement
Possible target-organ disease in established hypertension
Possible clinical clues to a secondary cause

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Clinic readings elevated but validated out-of-office average not persistently elevated.
Clinic readings may be below threshold while home or ambulatory readings are elevated.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistance, relevant medicines, renal or endocrine clues.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness, stimulants, or measurement error; repeat under standardised conditions.

ruleIn.testName: Repeated standardised clinic blood-pressure measurement

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Repeated standardised clinic blood-pressure measurement — Persistent elevated blood pressure
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Repeat valid readings and compare with the current Saudi diagnostic threshold.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Avoids diagnosis from an isolated or technically inaccurate reading.

ruleIn.testName: Home or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained, white-coat or masked hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Compare out-of-office averages with clinic readings using the appropriate thresholds.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms the blood-pressure pattern before long-term management decisions.

ruleIn.testName: Serum creatinine and eGFR

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum creatinine and eGFR — Reduced kidney filtration
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised creatinine or reduced eGFR warrants assessment against prior results.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects renal involvement and provides a treatment-safety baseline.

ruleIn.testName: Serum potassium and sodium

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum potassium and sodium — Electrolyte disturbance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Low potassium may suggest a secondary cause or medicine effect.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identifies secondary-cause clues and informs safe medicine selection.

ruleIn.testName: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio — Renal albumin leakage
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised albumin excretion suggests kidney damage; confirm as appropriate.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identifies renal target-organ involvement and modifies risk assessment.

ruleIn.testName: Urinalysis

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Urinalysis — Haematuria, protein or abnormal urinary sediment
ruleIn.expectedFinding: An abnormal result directs renal evaluation.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Haematuria, protein or abnormal urinary sediment
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Looks for kidney disease as a cause or consequence of hypertension.

ruleIn.testName: 12-lead electrocardiogram

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Left-ventricular hypertrophy, ischaemic change or arrhythmia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Relevant ECG changes identify cardiac involvement; a normal ECG does not exclude it.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Left-ventricular hypertrophy, ischaemic change or arrhythmia
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assesses cardiac consequences and competing cardiovascular disease.

ruleIn.testName: Lipid profile and glycaemia assessment

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Lipid profile and glycaemia assessment — Dyslipidaemia or diabetes accompanying hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Abnormal lipid/glucose results change cardiovascular-risk assessment.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines coexisting modifiable risk factors.

ruleOut.testName: Aldosterone-renin testing when primary aldosteronism is suspected

references.title: MSD Manual Professional: Hypertension — Testing
references.edition: Online review updated February 2026; Saudi application awaiting review

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Aldosterone-renin testing when primary aldosteronism is suspected — Inappropriate aldosterone activity
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Interpret the ratio with potassium, medicines and sampling conditions.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Investigates resistant hypertension or relevant hypokalaemia under a specialist/local pathway.

ruleOut.testName: Plasma free metanephrines when pheochromocytoma is suspected

references.title: MSD Manual Professional: Hypertension — Testing
references.edition: Online review updated February 2026; Saudi application awaiting review

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Plasma free metanephrines when pheochromocytoma is suspected — Catecholamine excess
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Raised results need contextual interpretation and confirmatory assessment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Investigates suggestive episodic symptoms or other relevant clinical clues.

ruleOut.testName: Sleep study when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected

references.title: MSD Manual Professional: Hypertension — Testing
references.edition: Online review updated February 2026; Saudi application awaiting review

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Sleep study when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected — Sleep-related obstructive breathing events
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A diagnostic study establishes clinically important sleep-disordered breathing.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Tests a suspected contributor; it is not routine for every hypertensive patient.

pathophysiology.summary: Essential hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure without an identified secondary cause. It is often asymptomatic and increases cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and kidney risk.
keyMechanisms: Interactions among genetic, renal, vascular, neurohormonal, and environmental factors
Increased systemic vascular resistance and altered sodium-volume regulation
Cumulative pressure-related vascular and target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.title: Screen and measure accurately
actions: Use a validated device, correct cuff, and standardised seated measurement after rest.
Obtain repeat readings and document method, values, symptoms, and context.
Review medicines, supplements, stimulants, tobacco, pain, and acute illness.
Do not diagnose from one isolated value unless urgent circumstances require action.
Arrange repeat and out-of-office confirmation within a risk-appropriate interval.
Explain follow-up and symptoms needing urgent assessment.
branches.condition: Elevated screening measurement without acute symptoms

actions: Arrange immediate emergency assessment.
Avoid rapid unsupervised outpatient lowering.
branches.condition: Severe elevation with possible acute target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Preventive and primary-care encounters, or when indicated

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and assess risk
actions: Confirm sustained hypertension with repeated clinic and/or validated out-of-office readings.
Assess cardiovascular risk, kidney function, diabetes, lipids, smoking, and target-organ injury.
Investigate secondary causes when clinical indications are present.
Agree an individualised plan and follow-up interval.
Consider white-coat hypertension rather than labelling sustained disease.
Continue monitoring based on overall risk.
branches.condition: Out-of-office values are not persistently elevated

actions: Arrange targeted work-up and specialist input as appropriate.
Address urgent complications through emergency care.
branches.condition: Secondary cause or target-organ injury suspected

clinicalManagement.timeframe: After elevated screening readings

clinicalManagement.title: Reduce risk and provide ongoing care
actions: Offer lifestyle measures and treatment options under current local guidance.
Select medication when indicated based on comorbidities, renal function, pregnancy potential, contraindications, and preference.
Review pressure, adherence, adverse effects, renal function, and risk after treatment changes.
Escalate persistent uncontrolled readings or suspected complications.
Use a pregnancy-specific assessment and treatment pathway.
Review medicines promptly and involve obstetric care when indicated.
branches.condition: Pregnancy or pregnancy potential

actions: Confirm measurement technique and adherence; review interfering medicines and secondary causes.
Adjust treatment or refer under local guidance.
branches.condition: Pressure remains above agreed target

clinicalManagement.timeframe: After diagnosis and at regular follow-up

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange repeat clinic or out-of-office measurements and cardiovascular-risk review according to results, patient risk, and local guidance.
mdtReferrals: Primary care or family medicine
Dietitian or lifestyle support
Cardiology, nephrology, or endocrinology when indicated
Obstetrics for pregnancy-associated hypertension
lifestyleAndDiet: Discuss balanced eating and sodium reduction where appropriate.
Encourage regular activity, healthy weight goals, and tobacco cessation.
Discuss alcohol use consistent with health needs and local advice.
patientEducation: Explain that hypertension is often symptom-free and needs accurate measurement and follow-up.
Teach home-monitoring technique when used.
Explain urgent symptoms requiring immediate assessment.
dischargeCriteria: Measurement result, confirmation plan, and precautions are documented.
Acute target-organ injury is assessed and disposition determined.
Patient knows when blood pressure will be reassessed.

redFlags: Continuous severe pain or peritonism
Shock, fever with toxicity, or metabolic acidosis
Strangulated hernia
Free air or suspected bowel ischaemia
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Acute Bowel Obstruction, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Diffuse bowel dilation without a mechanical transition; consider medicines and recent illness/surgery.
Diarrhoea and absence of progressive distension may support an alternative.
Pain out of proportion or peritonism requires emergency action.

ruleIn.testName: CT abdomen/pelvis when indicated by the surgical team
ruleIn.modalityTarget: CT abdomen/pelvis when indicated by the surgical team — Obstruction level, transition point, closed loop or bowel compromise
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Dilated bowel with a transition point; reduced enhancement, free fluid or perforation features raise concern for compromised bowel.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Obstruction level, transition point, closed loop or bowel compromise
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines anatomy and complications that change the urgency and type of surgical intervention.

ruleIn.testName: Serum electrolytes and creatinine
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum electrolytes and creatinine — Dehydration, kidney injury and electrolyte losses
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Potassium or sodium disturbance and rising creatinine after vomiting or reduced intake.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Dehydration, kidney injury and electrolyte losses
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides a baseline for fluid replacement and correction of electrolyte losses.

ruleOut.testName: Lactate and blood gas when ischaemia or shock is suspected
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Lactate and blood gas when ischaemia or shock is suspected — Hypoperfusion and metabolic acidosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Raised lactate or acidosis increases concern; normal early results do not exclude bowel ischaemia.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports urgent reassessment alongside examination and imaging; it cannot safely exclude strangulation alone.

pathophysiology.summary: A mechanical blockage or dysmotility causes proximal dilation and fluid sequestration. A closed-loop obstruction can compromise venous and arterial supply, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: A mechanical blockage or dysmotility causes proximal dilation and fluid sequestration. A closed-loop obstruction can compromise venous and arterial supply, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess urgency, stability, and the person’s priorities
actions: Confirm the presenting concern, relevant timeline, baseline function, medicines, allergies, comorbidities, and the patient’s immediate priorities.
Assess the red flags above and use the current local escalation pathway if instability or rapid deterioration is present.
Explain uncertainty and involve the patient or appropriate decision-maker in a way suited to the setting.
Escalate immediately to the responsible senior or emergency team using the local pathway.
Stabilise and investigate in parallel; do not delay time-critical action for routine testing.
branches.condition: A red flag, instability, or rapid deterioration is present

actions: Proceed with focused assessment and shared planning.
Document the threshold for urgent reassessment.
branches.condition: The person is stable for a planned or longitudinal pathway

actions: Use the history, examination, and investigations listed above to confirm the likely process and assess important alternatives.

Record severity, uncertainty, and which findings would change the plan.

Treat reversible contributors and address access, communication, cultural, and functional barriers.

Document the shared decision and safety-net plan.

actions: Continue the plan with monitoring proportional to risk.
Provide clear instructions for expected course and warning symptoms.

clinicalManagement.title: Coordinate handover, education, and follow-up
actions: Provide a written plan stating the working diagnosis, key findings, medicines or interventions, monitoring, and who owns each next step.
Use teach-back to check that the patient or caregiver understands warning symptoms, follow-up, and how to obtain help.
Close the loop on pending results, referrals, and screening or prevention actions.
Arrange a higher level of care or supported transfer and send a structured clinical handover.
Confirm transport, caregiver, and communication needs where relevant.

actions: Confirm a feasible follow-up date and contact route.
Document when and how the plan should be reviewed or escalated.
branches.condition: The patient is ready for outpatient or continuing care

patientEducation: Explain acute bowel obstruction in plain language, including what is known, what remains uncertain, and how the plan will be reviewed.
Use teach-back for warning signs, medicines or monitoring, and the route to urgent help.
Invite questions and adapt written or interpreted information to the patient’s language, health literacy, and communication needs.

redFlags: Severe hypoxaemia or rising carbon dioxide with acidosis
Exhaustion, confusion, or silent chest
Haemodynamic instability
Sudden pleuritic pain or unilateral reduced breath sounds
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Acute Exacerbation of COPD, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever, focal findings, or infiltrate may indicate concurrent infection.
Congestion may coexist and change fluid or respiratory decisions.
Consider when onset, pain, hypoxaemia, or examination is disproportionate.

ruleIn.testName: Pulse oximetry
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pulse oximetry — Hypoxaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced oxygen saturation; oximetry does not measure carbon dioxide or exclude hypercapnia.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Guides titrated oxygen and identifies the need for blood-gas assessment.

ruleIn.testName: Arterial blood gas when respiratory failure is suspected
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arterial blood gas when respiratory failure is suspected — Hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised carbon dioxide with reduced pH indicates ventilatory failure; compare with prior results and repeat when clinically indicated.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Helps determine ventilatory support and monitor response to treatment.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph when clinically indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph when clinically indicated — Pneumonia, pneumothorax or pulmonary oedema
ruleOut.expectedFinding: New focal opacity, pleural air or congestion suggests a cause beyond an uncomplicated exacerbation.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies treatable mimics and complications that require a different pathway.

ruleOut.testName: 12-lead ECG when cardiac disease is suspected
ruleOut.modalityTarget: 12-lead ECG when cardiac disease is suspected — Ischaemia or arrhythmia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: New ischaemic changes or a significant rhythm disturbance; a normal ECG does not exclude coronary disease.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Cardiac disease may precipitate or mimic respiratory deterioration.

pathophysiology.summary: Airway inflammation and mucus increase expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation; infection or pollutants can worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Severe episodes may cause hypercapnia, fatigue, and respiratory muscle failure. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Airway inflammation and mucus increase expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation
infection or pollutants can worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Severe episodes may cause hypercapnia, fatigue, and respiratory muscle failure.

content.title: Acute Heart Failure and Pulmonary Oedema

redFlags: Severe hypoxaemia or exhaustion
Hypotension, cool peripheries, or shock
Ongoing ischaemic chest pain or dangerous arrhythmia
Altered consciousness or rapidly worsening respiratory distress
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Acute Heart Failure and Pulmonary Oedema, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever or focal findings may coexist with congestion.
Acute pleuritic symptoms and thromboembolic risk require structured assessment.
Wheeze does not exclude simultaneous cardiac congestion.

ruleIn.testName: Chest radiograph
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph — Pulmonary congestion and pleural effusions
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Interstitial or alveolar oedema and effusions may be present; absence does not exclude early heart failure.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assesses congestion and alternative thoracic causes of acute dyspnoea.

ruleIn.testName: Echocardiography
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Echocardiography — Ventricular dysfunction or an acute structural cause
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced ventricular function, important valve disease or other structural abnormality; preserved ejection fraction does not exclude heart failure.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Ventricular dysfunction or an acute structural cause
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines the cardiac phenotype and detects causes needing urgent specialist intervention.

ruleIn.testName: Creatinine and electrolytes
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine and electrolytes — Kidney dysfunction and sodium/potassium disturbance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Renal impairment or electrolyte abnormality at baseline or during treatment.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Informs safe diuresis, medication selection and monitoring.

ruleOut.testName: 12-lead ECG and troponin when ACS is suspected
ruleOut.modalityTarget: 12-lead ECG and troponin when ACS is suspected — Acute coronary ischaemia or a significant arrhythmia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Ischaemic ECG changes or a troponin rise/fall require interpretation with symptoms; troponin may rise in heart failure without ACS.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary ischaemia or a significant arrhythmia
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies a precipitant requiring a parallel cardiac emergency pathway.

pathophysiology.summary: Raised filling pressures cause pulmonary or systemic venous congestion; impaired output and neurohormonal activation can worsen renal sodium retention. Acute triggers may include ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled blood pressure, medication interruption, or renal deterioration. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Raised filling pressures cause pulmonary or systemic venous congestion

impaired output and neurohormonal activation can worsen renal sodium retention. Acute triggers may include ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled blood pressure, medication interruption, or renal deterioration.

Refractory hyperkalaemia or acidosis
Pulmonary oedema or uraemic complication

redFlags: Chest pain, focal neurological deficit, severe breathlessness or syncope discovered during screening
Markedly elevated blood pressure with acute target-organ symptoms
Suicidal ideation or immediate safeguarding concern
Alarm cancer symptoms such as unexplained bleeding, persistent mass or major unintentional weight loss
symptoms: Often asymptomatic attendance for preventive review
May disclose fatigue, low mood, sleep problems or reduced function during structured history
May report tobacco exposure, inactivity, unhealthy diet or occupational risk
May have overdue vaccination or cancer screening
physicalSigns: Elevated or discrepant blood-pressure readings
Raised body-mass index or waist circumference
Oral-health, vision, hearing or mobility concerns
Abnormal findings requiring conversion from screening to a diagnostic pathway

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Asymptomatic, eligible by age or risk and suitable for a validated screening intervention.
Known diagnosis or repeated abnormal result requiring disease-specific targets rather than screening thresholds.
Symptoms or signs raise pre-test probability and require diagnostic, not screening, tests.
Single clinic value is not confirmed on repeat or out-of-office measurement.

ruleIn.testName: Standardised blood-pressure measurement with out-of-office confirmation
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standardised blood-pressure measurement with out-of-office confirmation — Hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Persistently elevated readings confirmed outside the clinic when indicated.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Reduces misclassification from technique, white-coat effect and isolated readings.

ruleIn.testName: Risk-based glucose testing
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Risk-based glucose testing — Prediabetes or diabetes
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Abnormal fasting glucose, random glucose in context or glycated haemoglobin confirmed through the diagnostic pathway.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: PHA guidance begins routine adult testing at the defined age and earlier with overweight plus risk factors.

ruleIn.testName: Age-, sex- and risk-appropriate cancer screening
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Age-, sex- and risk-appropriate cancer screening — Preclinical breast, colorectal, cervical or lung cancer
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Negative screening at the recommended interval or an abnormal result requiring timely diagnostic confirmation.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Preclinical breast, colorectal, cervical or lung cancer
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Benefit depends on eligibility, interval and complete follow-through after an abnormal screen.

ruleOut.testName: Repeat or confirmatory diagnostic test after an abnormal screen
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Repeat or confirmatory diagnostic test after an abnormal screen — False-positive screening result
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Diagnostic testing does not confirm disease.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Screening tests do not by themselves establish many diagnoses.

ruleOut.testName: Medication and comorbidity review
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Medication and comorbidity review — Secondary or iatrogenic risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A medicine, pregnancy state, renal disease or other condition explains or changes the preventive finding.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Prevents inappropriate application of general-population screening or treatment advice.

pathophysiology.summary: Periodic health examination is a risk-based preventive-care process rather than a disease episode. It identifies modifiable cardiovascular, metabolic, cancer, infectious, mental-health and functional risks before symptoms or irreversible complications develop, while avoiding screening that has an unfavourable balance of benefit and harm.
keyMechanisms: Age, sex, family history, exposures and comorbidity alter baseline disease probability and screening benefit.
Repeated measurement can detect trajectories in blood pressure, adiposity, glycaemia and lipids before complications emerge.
Evidence-based screening shifts selected cancers and chronic diseases toward earlier diagnosis.
Shared decisions reduce harms from false positives, overdiagnosis and preventive medicines with small net benefit.

clinicalManagement.title: Build an individual risk inventory
actions: Record age, sex, pregnancy potential, family history, tobacco exposure, occupation, medicines, comorbidity and prior screening.
Assess mental health, safety, function and social determinants with validated tools where appropriate.
Separate asymptomatic screening from symptoms that require diagnostic evaluation.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At each periodic examination

clinicalManagement.title: Complete core measurements
actions: Measure blood pressure using validated technique and assess body-mass index and waist circumference at the PHA interval.
Order glucose and lipid testing according to age and risk.
Review oral health, vaccination status and age-related vision, hearing, falls or cognition needs.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During the visit

clinicalManagement.title: Offer eligible screening
actions: Offer breast, cervical, colorectal, lung, osteoporosis and abdominal-aortic-aneurysm screening only when age, sex and risk criteria are met.
Explain likely benefits, limitations and follow-up before testing.
Create a closed-loop plan for every abnormal result.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At the guideline-defined interval

clinicalManagement.title: Deliver preventive interventions
actions: Provide indicated immunisation under the current Saudi schedule.
Offer tobacco-cessation treatment, physical-activity and dietary support.
Use generic preventive pharmacotherapy only after formal cardiovascular-risk, contraindication and shared-decision assessment.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At the same visit or scheduled follow-up

clinicalManagement.title: Close the preventive-care loop
actions: Communicate normal and abnormal results in understandable language.
Convert confirmed abnormalities to the relevant diagnostic or chronic-care pathway.
Update the recall date and assign ownership for referrals and pending tests.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After results are available

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Maintain a personalised recall schedule based on the 2023 PHA age and risk tables, review abnormal results promptly, and update eligibility whenever health status, family history, pregnancy status or exposure changes.
mdtReferrals: Primary-care nurse or preventive-care coordinator for recall and result tracking
Dietitian, tobacco-cessation service or exercise professional according to risk
Mental-health service for confirmed depression, anxiety or safety concern
Diagnostic specialty pathway for any abnormal screening result
lifestyleAndDiet: Support a sustainable dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains and minimally processed foods while accounting for culture and comorbidity.
Encourage regular aerobic and strengthening activity adapted to ability.
Provide tobacco cessation, sleep, weight and oral-health support without stigma.
patientEducation: Explain that preventive tests are selected by personal risk and that more testing is not always safer.
Use shared decision making for preference-sensitive cancer screening and preventive medicines.
Give accessible instructions for preparation, result access and the next step after an abnormal result.
dischargeCriteria: Risk profile, due interventions and deferred shared decisions are documented.
Every test and referral has a named owner and result-communication method.
Urgent symptoms or severe abnormalities have been diverted to immediate assessment.

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, shock, ongoing myocardial ischaemia or severe pulmonary oedema
New focal neurological deficit suggesting stroke
Syncope with a very rapid or very slow ventricular response
Acute decompensated heart failure or pre-excited atrial fibrillation
symptoms: Palpitations or an irregular heartbeat
Breathlessness or reduced exercise tolerance
Fatigue, dizziness, presyncope or syncope
Chest discomfort or presentation with stroke or transient ischaemic attack
physicalSigns: Irregularly irregular pulse
Variable first heart sound and pulse deficit
Tachycardia or, with conduction disease or medication, bradycardia
Signs of heart failure, valve disease or systemic embolism

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Organised flutter activity on electrocardiogram, often with a regular or patterned ventricular response.
Discrete premature P waves with intervening sinus rhythm rather than sustained fibrillatory activity.
At least three P-wave morphologies and an isoelectric baseline, often in severe pulmonary disease.
Consistent P waves and a physiological trigger; careful lead review separates artefact from atrial activity.

ruleIn.testName: 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Atrial fibrillation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals with no consistent discrete P waves.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides rhythm confirmation and identifies conduction, ischaemic or pre-excitation features that alter management.

ruleIn.testName: Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring — Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Intermittent electrocardiographically documented atrial fibrillation during symptoms or silent episodes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Monitoring duration should match symptom frequency when the resting electrocardiogram is normal.

ruleIn.testName: Transthoracic echocardiography when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Transthoracic echocardiography when indicated — Structural or functional heart disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Atrial enlargement, ventricular dysfunction, valve disease or another finding that changes management.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports rhythm-control planning, heart-failure assessment and selected refinement of thromboembolic risk.

ruleOut.testName: Thyroid function testing
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Thyroid function testing — Thyrotoxicosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No biochemical hyperthyroidism, or a reversible driver is identified.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Thyroid disease can precipitate atrial fibrillation and requires concurrent treatment.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, renal and liver function
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, renal and liver function — Metabolic precipitant or medicine contraindication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No correctable electrolyte disturbance; organ function is adequate for the selected medicine or prompts adjustment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies reversible contributors and is essential before anticoagulant or antiarrhythmic selection.

ruleOut.testName: Acute coronary and pulmonary assessment when clinically indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Acute coronary and pulmonary assessment when clinically indicated — Acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No acute ischaemic or thromboembolic trigger, or one is identified and treated through its urgent pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: New atrial fibrillation may be secondary to another time-critical condition.

pathophysiology.summary: Atrial fibrillation is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia with disorganised atrial activation and ineffective atrial contraction. Irregular ventricular conduction can cause symptoms or tachycardia-mediated dysfunction, while atrial blood stasis promotes thrombus formation and systemic embolism.
keyMechanisms: Ectopic atrial triggers and a susceptible atrial substrate sustain chaotic electrical activation.
Loss of coordinated atrial contraction and irregular atrioventricular conduction reduce haemodynamic efficiency.
Blood stasis, endothelial dysfunction and prothrombotic factors increase left-atrial thrombus and stroke risk.
Hypertension, heart failure, valve disease, thyroid disease, obesity, sleep apnoea and alcohol can promote onset or recurrence.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess stability and reversible triggers
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, ischaemia, heart failure and neurological status.
Obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram and correct hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance or another precipitant.
Seek senior cardiology/critical-care support for unstable or pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Perform urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion under the locally approved resuscitation and sedation protocol.
Do not delay emergency cardioversion solely to complete routine anticoagulation assessment.
branches.condition: Life-threatening haemodynamic instability attributable to atrial fibrillation

actions: Proceed to symptom, duration, rate/rhythm and thromboembolic-risk assessment.
branches.condition: No life-threatening instability

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately at acute presentation

clinicalManagement.title: Assess stroke and bleeding risks
actions: Use CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk and a validated bleeding-risk tool such as ORBIT.
Identify and modify reversible bleeding risks rather than using a bleeding score alone to withhold anticoagulation.
Discuss absolute benefits, bleeding harms and patient preferences using shared decision making.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis and whenever risk factors change

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent thromboembolism
actions: Offer an SFDA-authorised generic direct-acting oral anticoagulant, such as dabigatran etexilate or rivaroxaban, when indicated and suitable; select using renal function, interactions, adherence and the local formulary.
Use warfarin when a direct-acting anticoagulant is contraindicated, unsuitable, or the clinical condition specifically requires a vitamin-K antagonist.
Do not use antiplatelet monotherapy solely for atrial-fibrillation stroke prevention.
Use current SFDA labelling and the local formulary for all dosing; this record is not a prescribing source.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly after risk assessment

clinicalManagement.title: Choose rate or rhythm control
actions: Use rate control first for many stable patients, with a generic beta-blocker or rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker selected for comorbidity and contraindications.
Consider rhythm control for persistent symptoms, a reversible cause, new onset, atrial flutter suitable for ablation or heart failure thought to be driven by the arrhythmia.
Avoid a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker in acute decompensated heart failure and obtain specialist advice.
Assess anticoagulation requirements around cardioversion according to rhythm duration and the current protocol.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During initial management and at symptom review

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate persistent or complex disease
actions: Refer for cardiology review when symptoms remain uncontrolled, recurrence follows cardioversion or antiarrhythmic/ablation decisions are needed.
Consider catheter ablation through specialist shared decision making for eligible symptomatic patients.
Reassess stroke prevention after rhythm restoration because apparent sinus rhythm does not automatically remove thromboembolic risk.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly when initial treatment fails or complexity is identified

content.title: Gestational Diabetes Identification and Management Pathway
content.specialty: Obstetrics, Maternal-Fetal Medicine, and Diabetes Care

redFlags: Marked hyperglycaemia with vomiting, dehydration, altered mental status, or ketones
Reduced fetal movement, bleeding, or severe abdominal pain
Symptoms concerning for pre-eclampsia
symptoms: Often asymptomatic and detected through antenatal screening
Possible increased thirst or urination, which may overlap with normal pregnancy changes
physicalSigns: Usually no specific examination finding
Risk factors may include previous gestational diabetes, prior macrosomia, obesity, or family history

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Hyperglycaemia meeting overt diabetes criteria early in pregnancy or evidence predating pregnancy.
Elevated glucose during acute illness or medication exposure; interpret timing and repeat as appropriate.
Thirst or urinary frequency without diagnostic hyperglycaemia; symptoms alone do not establish GDM.

ruleIn.testName: Pregnancy-specific oral glucose tolerance test using local protocol
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pregnancy-specific oral glucose tolerance test using local protocol — Gestational diabetes
ruleIn.expectedFinding: One or more glucose values meet locally adopted diagnostic thresholds
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Apply the approved screening and diagnostic protocol consistently.

ruleIn.testName: Laboratory fasting or random plasma glucose when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Laboratory fasting or random plasma glucose when indicated — Overt diabetes in pregnancy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Value meets accepted overt-diabetes criteria or local pregnancy pathway
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identify significant hyperglycaemia that may represent pre-existing diabetes.

ruleIn.testName: Serial self-monitored blood glucose
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial self-monitored blood glucose — Glycaemic control during pregnancy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Repeated readings outside individualised targets
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Guide timely adjustment and assess response.

ruleIn.testName: Obstetric ultrasound when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Obstetric ultrasound when indicated — Fetal growth or fluid concern
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Growth or fluid finding requiring obstetric review
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess pregnancy concerns and guide obstetric planning.

ruleOut.testName: Pregnancy-specific oral glucose tolerance test using local protocol
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Pregnancy-specific oral glucose tolerance test using local protocol — Gestational diabetes
ruleOut.expectedFinding: All measured values below adopted diagnostic thresholds
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: A correctly timed test can exclude GDM at that screening point.

ruleOut.testName: Repeat glucose assessment when initial testing is incomplete or concern persists
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Repeat glucose assessment when initial testing is incomplete or concern persists — Missed or evolving gestational hyperglycaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Repeat values below diagnostic thresholds under appropriate protocol
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Consider timing, risk, test quality, and evolving pregnancy.

pathophysiology.summary: Gestational diabetes is glucose intolerance first recognised during pregnancy. Pregnancy-related insulin resistance may exceed pancreatic insulin-secretory capacity, increasing maternal glucose and fetal exposure.
keyMechanisms: Placental hormones increase maternal insulin resistance
Insufficient compensatory insulin secretion leads to hyperglycaemia
Maternal glucose crosses the placenta and may affect fetal growth and perinatal risk

clinicalManagement.title: Screen, diagnose, and communicate
actions: Review diabetes history, prior GDM, pregnancy history, medicines, and risk factors.
Use the locally adopted pregnancy-specific screening and diagnostic protocol.
Distinguish GDM from overt pre-existing diabetes when early or marked hyperglycaemia is found.
Communicate results promptly to patient and antenatal team.
Arrange urgent obstetric-diabetes or emergency assessment based on status.
Use pregnancy-specific acute management guidance.
branches.condition: Overt diabetes, severe hyperglycaemia, or acute metabolic illness suspected

actions: Refer promptly to obstetric-diabetes care.
Provide initial education and arrange monitoring and review.
branches.condition: GDM diagnosed without acute instability

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At timing defined by local antenatal protocol

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor glucose and individualise treatment
actions: Teach self-monitoring and agree pregnancy-specific targets with the team.
Offer nutrition counselling and safe activity advice.
Review glucose records, symptoms, treatment tolerance, and obstetric concerns.
If targets are unmet, consider pregnancy-appropriate medicines under local protocol and specialist care.
Review technique, nutrition, adherence barriers, and intercurrent illness.
Escalate treatment under pregnancy-specific local guidance.
branches.condition: Values remain above agreed targets

actions: Arrange immediate maternity triage or emergency assessment.
Do not defer assessment to routine diabetes follow-up.
branches.condition: Reduced fetal movement or another obstetric warning symptom

clinicalManagement.timeframe: From diagnosis through pregnancy

clinicalManagement.title: Plan birth and postpartum reassessment
actions: Coordinate timing and place of birth based on maternal control and fetal assessment.
Document intrapartum glucose and newborn-care plans under local policy.
Review glucose-lowering treatment after delivery as requirements may change.
Arrange postpartum testing and longer-term primary-care follow-up.
Arrange timely medical assessment and diagnostic testing.
Continue the appropriate diabetes-care pathway.
branches.condition: Persistent postpartum hyperglycaemia or pre-existing diabetes concern

actions: Still arrange postpartum testing at the locally recommended interval.
Discuss future risk reduction and screening in subsequent pregnancies.
branches.condition: Glucose normalises after birth

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Later pregnancy, birth, and after delivery

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Continue antenatal review based on glucose control and obstetric risk; arrange postpartum testing according to local protocol and ongoing primary-care screening.
mdtReferrals: Obstetric or maternal-fetal medicine team
Diabetes nurse or educator
Dietitian
Neonatal team when indicated
Primary care or diabetes service postpartum
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer culturally appropriate nutrition advice supporting pregnancy and glucose management.
Encourage safe regular activity when not contraindicated.
Avoid restrictive diets or weight-loss advice during pregnancy unless directed by the team.
patientEducation: Explain GDM, monitoring, and how results guide parent and baby care.
Teach monitoring and whom to contact for repeated out-of-range readings.
Provide maternity warning signs including reduced fetal movement.
dischargeCriteria: Maternal and fetal status are appropriate for planned setting.
Patient has monitoring instructions, contact routes, and follow-up plan.
Postpartum testing responsibilities are documented before birth discharge.

content.title: Palliative Management of End-of-Life Dyspnoea and Pain

redFlags: New potentially reversible emergency consistent with goals of care
Sudden severe dyspnoea, airway obstruction, major bleeding, or rapidly worsening consciousness
Uncontrolled pain or dyspnoea despite plan
Suspected medication toxicity or administration error
symptoms: Subjective breathlessness, air hunger, or breathing-related distress
Pain reported by patient or inferred from behaviour when communication is limited
Anxiety, restlessness, sleep disruption, or reduced function
physicalSigns: Increased work of breathing, altered respiratory rate, or accessory-muscle use
Guarding, grimacing, vocalisation, or reduced movement
Possible agitation, altered alertness, or signs of underlying illness

differentials.condition: Acute reversible respiratory or cardiac illness
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt onset, new examination findings, or treatable cause; assess when consistent with goals.

differentials.condition: Anxiety or panic contributing to dyspnoea
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Prominent fear or episodic distress may contribute, but physical causes still merit consideration.
Fluctuating attention or altered cognition; use observational assessment and collateral history.
Temporal association with medicine change, sedation, confusion, respiratory suppression, or other adverse effect.

ruleIn.testName: Patient-reported symptom assessment or validated observational tool
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Patient-reported symptom assessment or validated observational tool — Clinically significant pain or dyspnoea
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reported or observed distress requiring an individualised comfort plan
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Measure symptoms in a way suited to communication ability and reassess response.

ruleIn.testName: Focused history, examination, and medication review
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Focused history, examination, and medication review — Potentially treatable symptom contributor
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Clinical evidence identifying a cause or medicine-related factor
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identify reversible causes when assessment and treatment align with goals.

ruleIn.testName: Targeted investigation after goals-of-care discussion
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Targeted investigation after goals-of-care discussion — Specific suspected reversible cause
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Result likely to change a goal-concordant plan
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Avoid burdensome testing unlikely to improve comfort or alter decisions.

ruleOut.testName: Medication reconciliation and focused reassessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Medication reconciliation and focused reassessment — Medication-related toxicity
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No significant medication association or toxicity signs
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Review medicines and recent changes before escalating symptom treatment.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted assessment for suspected reversible emergency
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted assessment for suspected reversible emergency — Acute reversible cause requiring urgent treatment
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No evidence of suspected cause on proportionate assessment
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute reversible cause requiring urgent treatment
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Select investigations likely to change a goal-concordant plan; no test excludes every cause.

pathophysiology.summary: Dyspnoea and pain are distressing symptoms in serious illness. At end of life they may arise from disease, complications, treatment effects, or interacting causes; care should reflect patient goals.
keyMechanisms: Dyspnoea may reflect respiratory, cardiac, metabolic, psychological, or multifactorial processes
Pain may arise from tissue injury, inflammation, nerve involvement, or disease-related pressure
Fear, fatigue, delirium, and caregiver distress may amplify symptoms

clinicalManagement.title: Assess distress, goals, and reversible contributors
actions: Ask about symptom severity, comfort goals, fears, and preferred support; use an observational tool if needed.
Review care plan, advance-care documentation, capacity, and expressed goals.
Assess reversible contributors and review medicines, allergies, organ function, and prior responses.
Include family or caregivers with consent and respect privacy and cultural preferences.
Arrange urgent assessment and treatment through the appropriate pathway.
Continue comfort measures and communicate the plan.
branches.condition: Potentially reversible emergency identified and treatment aligns with goals

actions: Use proportionate assessment focused on acceptable comfort measures.
Document goals, limits, and escalation preferences.
branches.condition: Comfort is the priority and burdensome tests would not change care

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At escalation and whenever the situation changes

clinicalManagement.title: Provide individualised symptom relief
actions: Use positioning, calm presence, airflow or a fan when acceptable, and other low-burden measures.
Follow the local palliative formulary and senior guidance; individualise medicines to prior exposure, organ function, route, and goals.
Assess pain type and use appropriate non-pharmacological and pharmacological measures.
Reassess comfort, alertness, adverse effects, and patient preferences.
Request urgent palliative or senior review.
Reconsider setting, route, cause, and proportionality of further intervention.
branches.condition: Severe symptoms persist despite initial plan

actions: Arrange prompt clinical review for toxicity or other causes.
Adjust or withhold medicines only through responsible clinician and local protocol.
branches.condition: Sedation, confusion, respiratory suppression, or adverse effect suspected

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly, with reassessment after each intervention

clinicalManagement.title: Coordinate continuing care and support
actions: Agree a written symptom plan, contacts, worsening-symptom steps, and preferred place of care when feasible.
Ensure access to prescribed medicines, equipment, and trained support.
Coordinate patient, family, palliative, primary-care, and specialist communication.
Review caregiver burden and psychosocial, cultural, and spiritual needs.
Arrange urgent specialist review and consider transfer consistent with goals.
Provide structured handover of symptoms, medicines, response, allergies, and preferences.
branches.condition: Symptoms cannot be safely controlled in current setting

actions: Continue documented comfort plan and scheduled review.
Provide caregivers clear contact details and practical support.
branches.condition: Symptoms acceptably controlled in preferred setting

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Throughout care and at transitions

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange palliative follow-up based on symptom burden and setting, with an urgent route for worsening pain, dyspnoea, or adverse effects.
mdtReferrals: Palliative-care physician and nurse
Primary-care or treating specialist team
Clinical pharmacist
Psychology, social work, or spiritual care by preference
Home healthcare or hospice when available and appropriate
Family and caregiver support
lifestyleAndDiet: Prioritise comfort, rest, preferred food and fluids as tolerated, and patient choices.
Offer positioning, calm environment, and activity pacing to reduce distress.
patientEducation: Explain palliative care aims to relieve suffering and support patient and family.
Describe comfort measures and how to use the symptom plan and contact the team.
Invite discussion of preferences, privacy, culture, and spiritual support.
dischargeCriteria: Symptoms acceptably controlled for chosen setting or safe transfer arranged.
Patient and caregivers understand symptom plan, medicine instructions, and contact route.
Goals, escalation preferences, and handover are documented and communicated.

redFlags: Silent chest
Exhaustion or altered consciousness
Cyanosis or severe hypoxemia
Poor respiratory effort
Hypotension or possible anaphylaxis
symptoms: Worsening dyspnea
Wheeze
Cough
Chest tightness
Reduced ability to speak or perform usual activity

content.title: Acute Anaphylaxis
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine and Allergy and Immunology

redFlags: Airway swelling, stridor, severe bronchospasm or rapidly worsening breathing
Hypotension, syncope, confusion or shock
Refractory symptoms after intramuscular epinephrine
Known mast-cell disorder, severe asthma, beta-blocker use or prior biphasic/refractory anaphylaxis
symptoms: Sudden throat tightness, hoarse voice or difficulty swallowing
Breathlessness, wheeze or persistent cough
Generalised itching, flushing, urticaria or swelling
Dizziness, collapse, cramping abdominal pain or vomiting after a likely exposure
physicalSigns: Stridor, angioedema or respiratory distress
Wheeze, hypoxaemia or reduced air entry
Hypotension, tachycardia, poor perfusion or collapse
Generalised urticaria or flushing, noting that skin signs can be absent

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Predominantly lower-airway obstruction without hypotension, acute skin/mucosal change or a clear multisystem exposure response.
Bradycardia, pallor and rapid improvement supine without urticaria, wheeze or airway swelling.
Angioedema without urticaria, often slower onset and limited response to epinephrine or antihistamine.
Infective syndrome and less immediate exposure relationship, although initial shock management may overlap.

ruleIn.testName: Clinical diagnostic criteria
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Clinical diagnostic criteria — Anaphylaxis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Acute airway, breathing or circulatory compromise with compatible skin/mucosal findings or a likely allergen exposure.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis and treatment must not wait for laboratory confirmation.

ruleIn.testName: Serial serum tryptase when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial serum tryptase when indicated — Systemic mast-cell activation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A rise above the person's baseline in an appropriately timed sample.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Can support later specialist evaluation but a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.

ruleOut.testName: Point-of-care glucose
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Point-of-care glucose — Hypoglycaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Glucose is not low enough to explain altered consciousness or collapse.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Rapidly excludes a reversible mimic while resuscitation continues.

ruleOut.testName: Electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram — Primary arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No primary electrical or ischaemic cause for collapse.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Primary arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Particularly important in older patients, chest pain, severe hypotension or epinephrine-related symptoms.

pathophysiology.summary: Anaphylaxis is a rapid systemic hypersensitivity reaction. Mast-cell and basophil mediator release causes vasodilation, capillary leak, mucosal oedema and bronchoconstriction, which can progress quickly to airway obstruction, distributive shock and cardiac arrest.
keyMechanisms: IgE-mediated or non-IgE pathways trigger widespread mediator release.
Vasodilation and capillary permeability reduce venous return and blood pressure.
Upper-airway oedema and lower-airway bronchospasm compromise ventilation.
Biphasic recurrence can occur after apparent initial resolution.

clinicalManagement.title: Give intramuscular epinephrine
actions: Administer intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh using the current MOH age/weight dosing protocol.
Repeat at the protocol interval if airway, breathing or circulatory compromise persists.
Do not delay epinephrine for antihistamines, corticosteroids, intravenous access or diagnostic tests.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Position and support airway and breathing
actions: Lay the patient flat with legs elevated unless respiratory distress requires a supported position; avoid sudden standing or sitting.
Call the resuscitation team, give high-concentration oxygen when indicated and prepare early for a difficult airway.
Use inhaled bronchodilator as an adjunct for persistent bronchospasm, never as a substitute for epinephrine.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Concurrent with first epinephrine dose

clinicalManagement.title: Restore circulation
actions: Establish intravenous or intraosseous access and give rapid isotonic crystalloid with frequent reassessment.
Use continuous monitoring and obtain senior critical-care support for refractory shock.
Intravenous epinephrine infusion is restricted to appropriately monitored settings and experienced clinicians.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately when shock is present

clinicalManagement.title: Stop exposure and add adjunctive care
actions: Stop the suspected trigger when this can be done safely, such as halting an infusion.
After stabilisation, use adjunctive antihistamine for persistent skin symptoms according to local policy.
Do not rely on corticosteroids to prevent immediate deterioration or replace observation.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as feasible

clinicalManagement.title: Observe and plan safe discharge
actions: Use risk-stratified observation, extending monitoring after severe, refractory or high-risk reactions.
Document the suspected trigger and all treatment times.
Provide an emergency plan and allergy referral before discharge.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After complete clinical resolution

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange allergy evaluation, ensure the event is recorded in the medicine/allergy record, review auto-injector availability before expiry, and advise immediate emergency care for any recurrent systemic reaction.
mdtReferrals: Allergy and immunology for trigger confirmation and prevention planning
Critical care for refractory airway, breathing or circulatory compromise
Dietitian for confirmed food allergy requiring substantial dietary exclusion
Pharmacy for auto-injector access and technique reinforcement
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid the suspected trigger until specialist assessment clarifies the diagnosis.
