Interpret results using current national/local diagnostic criteria, age, pregnancy status, comorbidity, and prior results.
Record severity, uncertainty, and which findings would change the plan.
Reassess the history and examination and seek senior or specialty advice.
Use targeted additional testing only when its result can change management.
branches.condition: The diagnosis remains uncertain or tests conflict with the clinical picture

actions: Switch to the relevant urgent or specialty pathway.
Communicate the finding and handover responsibility clearly.
branches.condition: A high-risk complication or an alternative diagnosis is identified

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly; adapt timing to acuity

clinicalManagement.title: Agree evidence-informed care and address the cause
actions: Use the topic-specific focus in this record to agree immediate and longer-term priorities with the patient.
Select treatment only after checking current local guidance, formulary, contraindications, interactions, organ function, pregnancy considerations, and patient preference.
Treat reversible contributors and address access, communication, cultural, and functional barriers.
Reassess diagnosis, treatment burden, adherence barriers, and alternatives with the responsible specialist.
Document the shared decision and safety-net plan.
branches.condition: Treatment is ineffective, poorly tolerated, or inconsistent with the patient’s goals

actions: Continue the plan with monitoring proportional to risk.
Provide clear instructions for expected course and warning symptoms.
branches.condition: The patient improves on the agreed plan

clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to acuity and current local protocol

clinicalManagement.title: Coordinate handover, education, and follow-up
actions: Provide a written plan stating the working diagnosis, key findings, medicines or interventions, monitoring, and who owns each next step.
Use teach-back to check that the patient or caregiver understands warning symptoms, follow-up, and how to obtain help.
Close the loop on pending results, referrals, and screening or prevention actions.
Arrange a higher level of care or supported transfer and send a structured clinical handover.
Confirm transport, caregiver, and communication needs where relevant.
branches.condition: Safe care cannot be delivered in the current setting

actions: Confirm a feasible follow-up date and contact route.
Document when and how the plan should be reviewed or escalated.
branches.condition: The patient is ready for outpatient or continuing care

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before transition and at the agreed review interval

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review the topic-specific focus, patient goals, symptoms and function at an interval matched to risk. Reconcile new results and treatment effects, close referrals, and revisit the plan if the condition, circumstances, or preferences change.
mdtReferrals: Cardiology / Cardiothoracic Surgery
Primary care or the responsible continuity team
Pharmacist, nurse educator, dietitian, rehabilitation, mental-health, or social support when relevant to the case.
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer topic-relevant prevention or self-management support that is safe, feasible, culturally appropriate, and consistent with the person’s goals.
Avoid one-size-fits-all restrictions; individualise advice for pregnancy, frailty, kidney/heart disease, disability, and treatment burden.
patientEducation: Explain elective valve intervention assessment in plain language, including what is known, what remains uncertain, and how the plan will be reviewed.
Use teach-back for warning signs, medicines or monitoring, and the route to urgent help.
Invite questions and adapt written or interpreted information to the patient’s language, health literacy, and communication needs.
dischargeCriteria: Clinical status is appropriate for the next setting, and urgent complications have been excluded or addressed.
The patient or caregiver has an understandable plan, access to needed treatment/support, and a clear escalation route.
Pending investigations and referrals have a named owner and follow-up timeframe.

content.title: Hypertension in Adults [Adapted from NICE]
content.specialty: Family Medicine, Internal Medicine and Cardiology

redFlags: Blood pressure at or above the severe range with retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema, confusion, chest pain, acute kidney injury or heart failure
Pregnancy or possible pregnancy with severe hypertension or concerning symptoms
Acute focal neurological deficit or aortic-dissection features
Suspected catecholamine crisis or another rapidly progressive secondary cause
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic and detected on screening
Headache or dizziness, which are non-specific
Symptoms of target-organ disease such as exertional chest discomfort, breathlessness or neurological episodes
Features suggesting a secondary cause, including episodic palpitations, muscle weakness or sleep apnoea
physicalSigns: Repeated elevated clinic blood pressure using correct technique
Postural blood-pressure fall in older adults, diabetes or symptomatic patients
Retinal vascular change
Signs of left-ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease or endocrine disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Raised clinic readings with normal validated ambulatory or home averages.
Normal clinic readings but elevated out-of-office averages or unexplained target-organ damage.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistant disease, hypokalaemia, renal findings, endocrine features or a medicine/substance trigger.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness or recent stimulant exposure with normal readings after the driver resolves.

ruleIn.testName: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure — Persistent clinic hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Clinic blood pressure remains at or above the diagnostic threshold after repeat measurement with correct cuff and positioning.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Technique and repetition reduce random error and identify inter-arm difference.

ruleIn.testName: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average waking readings meet the validated diagnostic threshold using adequate measurements.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Preferred confirmation method for clinic readings below the severe range and distinguishes white-coat effect.

ruleIn.testName: Home blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average readings after discarding the first day meet the validated home threshold.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides confirmation and supports later self-monitoring when performed with a validated device and protocol.

ruleOut.testName: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis — Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No albuminuria or haematuria, or an abnormality prompts renal evaluation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Renal disease can be both a cause and consequence of hypertension and changes treatment choice and targets.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile — Secondary contributor and cardiovascular comorbidity
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Baseline metabolic and renal status is defined; hypokalaemia, kidney dysfunction or diabetes redirects assessment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports cardiovascular-risk estimation and safe medicine selection.

ruleOut.testName: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram — Retinal or cardiac target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No hypertensive retinopathy or left-ventricular/cardiac abnormality, or damage is documented for risk management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Target-organ damage changes urgency and the balance of treatment benefit.

pathophysiology.summary: Sustained arterial hypertension reflects increased systemic vascular resistance, altered sodium-volume balance and neurohormonal activation interacting with age, genetics, adiposity and environmental exposures. Chronic pressure load accelerates vascular remodelling and damages the heart, brain, kidneys, retina and peripheral arteries.
keyMechanisms: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic activation increase vascular tone and sodium retention.
Endothelial dysfunction and arterial stiffness raise systolic pressure and pulse pressure.
Renal sodium handling and pressure natriuresis reset at a higher arterial pressure.
Persistent load causes left-ventricular hypertrophy, albuminuria, retinopathy and cerebrovascular injury.

clinicalManagement.title: Measure and confirm
actions: Use a validated, maintained device, correct cuff size, supported arm and a quiet seated setting.
Measure both arms initially and use the arm with the persistently higher reading.
Confirm clinic hypertension with ambulatory monitoring or, when unsuitable, structured home monitoring unless urgent severe hypertension requires immediate assessment.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At initial and confirmation visits

clinicalManagement.title: Identify severe hypertension requiring urgent assessment
actions: Assess for retinal, neurological, cardiac, aortic and renal target-organ injury.
Use emergency transfer for life-threatening symptoms or suspected acute organ injury.
Do not rapidly lower asymptomatic blood pressure outside a monitored, indication-specific protocol.
Activate emergency specialist management and monitored intravenous therapy under the local protocol.
branches.condition: Severe blood pressure with acute target-organ injury

actions: Arrange urgent clinical review, confirm adherence and complete prompt organ assessment rather than routine follow-up.
branches.condition: Severe blood pressure without acute target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Same day when severe readings or symptoms are present

clinicalManagement.title: Assess cardiovascular risk and organ damage
actions: Obtain urine albumin-creatinine ratio, haematuria screen, glycated haemoglobin, electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR and lipids.
Perform fundoscopy and a 12-lead electrocardiogram.
Use a cardiovascular-risk tool validated or approved for local Saudi practice and assess for secondary-cause clues.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During diagnostic confirmation

clinicalManagement.title: Start lifestyle and pharmacological treatment
actions: Offer lifestyle intervention to every patient and discuss medicine using age, diabetes, kidney disease, pregnancy potential, frailty and cardiovascular risk.
Use generic ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-receptor blockers, calcium-channel blockers or thiazide-like diuretics in the guideline sequence when suitable and SFDA authorised.
Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an angiotensin-receptor blocker.
Use current SFDA labelling and the local formulary for dose, contraindication and monitoring decisions; this record is not a prescribing source.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After confirmed diagnosis, sooner when severity or organ damage requires

clinicalManagement.title: Titrate and monitor
actions: Check adherence, side effects, postural symptoms and validated clinic or home readings before intensification.
Monitor kidney function and electrolytes after renin-angiotensin system blockers, diuretics or mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists according to protocol.
Before labelling resistant hypertension, confirm out-of-office elevation, optimal tolerated triple therapy and adherence, then seek specialist input or use protocol-directed fourth-line treatment.
Individualise targets for frailty, multimorbidity and significant postural hypotension.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At defined intervals after each treatment change and at least annually once stable

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review after initiation or each medicine change until a stable target is achieved, then provide at least annual review of blood pressure, postural symptoms, lifestyle, adherence, adverse effects, renal function and evolving cardiovascular risk.
mdtReferrals: Primary-care pharmacist or nurse for adherence and home-monitoring support
Nephrology, endocrinology or hypertension specialist for suspected secondary or resistant hypertension
Obstetric medicine for pregnancy, pregnancy planning or postpartum hypertension
Dietitian, weight-management and smoking-cessation services according to need
lifestyleAndDiet: Reduce dietary sodium using culturally relevant food choices; avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes when kidney disease, diabetes or interacting medicines make them unsafe.
Encourage regular aerobic and strengthening activity and gradual weight reduction when indicated.
Limit excessive caffeine and alcohol, stop smoking and address sleep apnoea risk.
Do not recommend calcium, magnesium or potassium supplements solely to lower blood pressure.
patientEducation: Explain that hypertension is often silent but treatment reduces long-term cardiovascular and renal risk.
Teach validated home-monitoring technique and how to record readings without excessive repeated checking.
Discuss medicine purpose, common adverse effects, pregnancy precautions and when to seek urgent care.
dischargeCriteria: Hypertension is confirmed or excluded using an appropriate out-of-office pathway.
Target-organ and cardiovascular-risk assessment is complete or has a named owner.
Treatment, monitoring, individual target and urgent symptom advice are documented and understood.

redFlags: Exhaustion, confusion, drowsiness, cyanosis, hypotension or a silent chest
Inability to speak, worsening hypoxaemia or poor respiratory effort despite initial treatment
Normal or rising arterial carbon dioxide in a patient with severe respiratory distress
Previous near-fatal asthma, intensive-care admission or mechanical ventilation
symptoms: Rapidly worsening breathlessness
Wheeze or chest tightness
Cough, often after a viral, allergen or irritant exposure
Reduced response to the patient's usual reliever medicine
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea with prolonged expiration
Diffuse expiratory wheeze or, in near-fatal obstruction, a quiet chest
Accessory-muscle use and inability to complete sentences
Tachycardia with reduced peak expiratory flow compared with predicted or personal best

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt multisystem illness with urticaria, angioedema, hypotension or gastrointestinal symptoms after a likely exposure.
Orthopnoea, inspiratory crackles, raised jugular venous pressure or radiographic congestion rather than predominantly expiratory obstruction.
Pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, venous-thromboembolism risk factors or unexplained hypoxaemia with limited wheeze.
Sudden unilateral pleuritic pain, asymmetric breath sounds and hyper-resonance; tension physiology adds hypotension and tracheal deviation.

ruleIn.testName: Peak expiratory flow
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Peak expiratory flow — Severity of airflow obstruction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Marked reduction from predicted or documented personal best, with serial improvement after treatment supporting reversible obstruction.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides an objective trend when the patient can perform the manoeuvre safely.

ruleIn.testName: Continuous pulse oximetry
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Continuous pulse oximetry — Hypoxaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced oxygen saturation or a need for supplemental oxygen to maintain the locally defined target.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects gas-exchange impairment and guides titrated oxygen while avoiding delay to treatment.

ruleIn.testName: Arterial or venous blood gas when severe or deteriorating
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arterial or venous blood gas when severe or deteriorating — Respiratory failure and metabolic disturbance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Hypoxaemia; carbon-dioxide retention or acidaemia in life-threatening disease.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: A rising carbon dioxide level can signal fatigue and the need for critical-care escalation.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph when clinically indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph when clinically indicated — Pneumothorax, pneumonia or pulmonary oedema
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No focal alternative pathology in uncomplicated asthma; an abnormality redirects management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Imaging is selective rather than routine and should not delay immediate bronchodilator treatment.

ruleOut.testName: 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Acute coronary syndrome or significant arrhythmia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Absence of acute ischaemic change or a clinically important rhythm disturbance.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or significant arrhythmia
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Useful for older patients, chest pain, marked tachycardia or relevant cardiovascular comorbidity.

pathophysiology.summary: An acute exacerbation is a sustained worsening of airflow obstruction caused by bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, airway-wall oedema and mucus plugging on a background of variable airway inflammation. Severe obstruction raises the work of breathing, produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and may progress from hypocapnia to carbon-dioxide retention as respiratory muscles fatigue.
keyMechanisms: Trigger-driven airway inflammation and bronchial hyper-responsiveness narrow conducting airways.
Mucosal oedema and tenacious secretions amplify expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation.
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; a normalising or rising carbon dioxide level in a distressed patient can indicate fatigue.
Prolonged expiration and air trapping increase intrathoracic pressure and the work of breathing.

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate assessment and stabilisation
actions: Use an airway-breathing-circulation approach and call senior emergency support for severe or life-threatening features.
Position upright when tolerated, establish monitoring and obtain intravenous access without delaying inhaled therapy.
Give controlled oxygen to the locally approved saturation target and reassess frequently.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately on arrival

clinicalManagement.title: Reverse bronchoconstriction
actions: Give repeated inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist using an appropriate delivery system.
Add inhaled ipratropium bromide in severe or life-threatening exacerbation.
Document response using symptoms, respiratory effort, oxygenation and peak flow where feasible.
Escalate immediately to a senior emergency/critical-care clinician.
Consider continuous nebulised bronchodilator delivery and intravenous magnesium sulfate under the approved local protocol.
branches.condition: Poor response or deteriorating physiology

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within minutes

clinicalManagement.title: Treat airway inflammation
actions: Administer systemic corticosteroid promptly unless contraindicated.
Review likely trigger, adherence and recent corticosteroid exposure.
Do not use antibiotics routinely unless bacterial infection is clinically supported.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Early in the first hour

clinicalManagement.title: Structured reassessment
actions: Repeat respiratory rate, work of breathing, speech, oxygen saturation and peak flow where possible.
Check for complications and alternative diagnoses if the trajectory is not improving.
Escalate for ventilatory support planning before exhaustion or reduced consciousness develops.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After each initial treatment cycle

clinicalManagement.title: Determine safe disposition
actions: Admit patients with persistent severe features, oxygen requirement, poor social support or high relapse risk.
Before discharge, verify inhaler technique, provide an individualised written action plan and arrange controller therapy review.
Explain explicit emergency return precautions.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After sustained clinical response

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange prompt primary-care or respiratory review after discharge, with earlier assessment for recurrent symptoms; review the trigger, control, adherence, inhaler technique and need to step up long-term therapy.
mdtReferrals: Respiratory specialist for life-threatening, recurrent severe or diagnostically uncertain asthma
Asthma educator or respiratory pharmacist for technique and adherence review
Critical care when deterioration, exhaustion or ventilatory support is anticipated
lifestyleAndDiet: Identify and reduce exposure to tobacco smoke, vaping, occupational irritants and known allergens.
Support influenza vaccination and other indicated immunisation under the Saudi schedule.
Encourage gradual return to activity once symptoms and peak flow recover.
patientEducation: Explain reliever versus controller medicines and the danger of relying on frequent reliever use.
Demonstrate inhaler and spacer technique and confirm understanding using teach-back.
Provide a written action plan that states deterioration thresholds and where to obtain urgent care.
dischargeCriteria: Symptoms and work of breathing have improved and remain stable after observation.
Oxygenation is stable without unplanned escalation and objective airflow is improving.
Medicines, inhaler technique, written action plan, follow-up and return precautions are confirmed.

content.title: Sepsis
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Critical Care

redFlags: Persistent hypotension or evidence of hypoperfusion after initial fluid resuscitation
New altered consciousness, rapidly increasing oxygen need or respiratory failure
Lactate elevation with clinical deterioration or oliguria
Purpura, necrotising soft-tissue features, meningism or a source needing immediate surgical control
symptoms: Fever, rigors or feeling unusually cold
New confusion, profound weakness or reduced urine output
Breathlessness, cough, dysuria, abdominal pain or another focal infection symptom
Rapid deterioration in a patient with recent infection, procedure or immunosuppression
physicalSigns: Altered mental status
Tachypnoea, hypoxaemia or increased work of breathing
Hypotension, prolonged capillary refill, mottling or cool peripheries
Oliguria, tachycardia or abnormal temperature

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ischaemic symptoms, pulmonary congestion, elevated jugular venous pressure or cardiac imaging suggesting pump failure.
History of bleeding or fluid loss without a convincing infectious focus; response depends on correction of the volume deficit.
Abrupt onset after exposure with skin or mucosal findings, bronchospasm or gastrointestinal symptoms.
Sudden dyspnoea or pleuritic pain, thromboembolic risk and right-heart strain without a clear infection syndrome.

ruleIn.testName: Serum lactate with repeat trend
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum lactate with repeat trend — Tissue hypoperfusion
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Elevation or failure to clear in a clinically deteriorating patient.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports severity assessment and response monitoring but must be interpreted with the whole clinical picture.

ruleIn.testName: Blood cultures and source-directed microbiology
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood cultures and source-directed microbiology — Causative infection
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Growth or molecular detection of a plausible pathogen from blood or the suspected source.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Enables antimicrobial narrowing and source-directed care; obtain before antibiotics only when this does not cause harmful delay.

ruleIn.testName: Organ-function panel
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Organ-function panel — Sepsis-associated organ dysfunction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Acute kidney, liver, coagulation, haematological or gas-exchange abnormality.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines severity, guides support and provides a baseline for trends.

ruleOut.testName: Electrocardiogram and cardiac biomarkers when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram and cardiac biomarkers when indicated — Acute coronary syndrome or primary cardiac shock
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No primary ischaemic pattern explaining the haemodynamic state.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or primary cardiac shock
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Cardiac disease can mimic or coexist with sepsis and changes fluid and vasopressor decisions.

ruleOut.testName: Source-directed imaging
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Source-directed imaging — Non-infectious mimic or drainable focus
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Imaging identifies or excludes pneumonia, obstruction, perforation, abscess or another urgent source.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Confirms anatomy and determines whether procedural source control is required.

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Endothelial injury, vasodilation, capillary leak, microvascular thrombosis and cellular metabolic dysfunction can impair tissue oxygen delivery and progress to shock and multiorgan failure.
keyMechanisms: An uncontrolled inflammatory and immune response disrupts endothelial integrity and vascular tone.
Relative and absolute hypovolaemia reduce effective circulating volume.
Microcirculatory dysfunction and coagulation activation impair organ perfusion.
Myocardial depression and cellular oxygen-utilisation defects can persist despite apparently corrected blood pressure.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise sepsis and grade urgency
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, perfusion and urine output.
Record observations and identify high-risk organ dysfunction without relying on a single screening score.
Activate senior and critical-care escalation for shock or rapidly worsening physiology.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Obtain time-critical diagnostics
actions: Measure lactate and obtain blood count, renal, liver, coagulation and glucose studies.
Take blood cultures and appropriate source specimens before antimicrobials when this can be done promptly.
Use targeted imaging to locate infection and source-control needs.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As early as possible without delaying treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Start infection and perfusion treatment
actions: Administer empiric intravenous antimicrobials selected for the suspected source, local resistance patterns, allergies and recent exposure.
Give balanced crystalloid in reassessed aliquots when hypoperfusion is present, accounting for cardiac or renal risk.
Provide oxygen and organ support according to measured need.
Start vasopressor support in a monitored setting under critical-care oversight.
Use dynamic reassessment to avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid overload.
branches.condition: Hypotension persists despite appropriate initial fluid

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately for shock or high-likelihood sepsis

clinicalManagement.title: Achieve source control
actions: Request surgical, interventional radiology or specialty review for drainage, debridement or device removal.
Do not defer an urgent source-control procedure solely to complete non-essential tests.
Document the source-control decision and planned timing.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently once the source is identified

clinicalManagement.title: Reassess and de-escalate
actions: Trend haemodynamics, lactate, urine output, oxygen need and organ function.
Review microbiology and narrow, change or stop antimicrobials when evidence supports it.
Reconsider the diagnosis and seek additional source control if improvement is inadequate.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Continuously, with formal review after initial resuscitation

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange source-appropriate clinical review and results follow-up, reconcile antimicrobials and other medicines, screen for post-sepsis functional or psychological problems, and escalate persistent fatigue, breathlessness, cognitive change or recurrent fever.
mdtReferrals: Critical care for shock, respiratory failure or escalating organ support
Source-specific surgical or procedural team
Microbiology or infectious diseases for complex infection or antimicrobial stewardship
Physiotherapy, dietetics and rehabilitation after prolonged or severe illness
lifestyleAndDiet: Support nutrition, hydration and mobilisation during recovery according to swallowing and organ-function assessment.
Review indicated vaccination and infection-prevention measures after the acute episode.
Address smoking and other modifiable infection risks when clinically stable.
patientEducation: Explain the suspected source, organ effects and why treatment and monitoring are time critical.
On recovery, provide signs of recurrent infection or deterioration that require urgent assessment.
Discuss antimicrobial purpose, planned review and potential adverse effects.
dischargeCriteria: Infection source and treatment plan are established with stable physiology.
Organ dysfunction has resolved or has a safe documented outpatient plan.
Oral therapy, monitoring, follow-up and explicit return precautions are feasible and understood.

content.title: Deep-Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine, Internal Medicine and Haematology

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, syncope with persistent hypotension or obstructive-shock features
Severe hypoxaemia, rapidly escalating oxygen requirement or cardiac arrest
Threatened limb with massive swelling, cyanosis or severe pain
Active major bleeding or another absolute barrier to anticoagulation in a patient with confirmed or highly suspected VTE
symptoms: Unilateral leg pain or swelling
Sudden unexplained dyspnoea
Pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis or syncope
Reduced exercise tolerance with recent immobility, surgery, cancer or prior thrombosis
physicalSigns: Unilateral pitting oedema, calf asymmetry or deep venous tenderness
Tachycardia, tachypnoea or hypoxaemia
Signs of right-heart strain such as raised jugular venous pressure
Hypotension or poor perfusion in high-risk pulmonary embolism

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Superficial erythema, warmth and a possible portal of entry with inflammatory features rather than isolated deep venous tenderness.
Posterior knee pathology with fluid tracking into the calf and diagnostic ultrasound findings.
Pressure-type pain, ischaemic electrocardiographic change or a coronary biomarker pattern rather than pleuritic pain and right-heart strain.
Focal infective symptoms or unilateral absent breath sounds with confirmatory chest imaging.

ruleIn.testName: Compression ultrasonography
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Compression ultrasonography — Proximal lower-limb DVT
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Non-compressible venous segment or directly visualised thrombus.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: First-line anatomical confirmation for suspected proximal DVT.

ruleIn.testName: CT pulmonary angiography
ruleIn.modalityTarget: CT pulmonary angiography — Pulmonary embolism
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Intraluminal filling defect in a pulmonary artery.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms pulmonary embolism and describes clot burden while also identifying some alternative thoracic diagnoses.

ruleIn.testName: Echocardiography in unstable PE
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Echocardiography in unstable PE — Right-ventricular pressure overload
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Right-ventricular dilatation or dysfunction compatible with acute pressure overload.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports urgent risk stratification when instability makes definitive imaging unsafe or delayed.

ruleOut.testName: High-sensitivity D-dimer in an appropriate low-probability pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: High-sensitivity D-dimer in an appropriate low-probability pathway — Acute VTE
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A negative result below the assay's validated threshold makes acute VTE unlikely in the selected population.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoids unnecessary imaging only after structured clinical-probability assessment.

ruleOut.testName: Ventilation-perfusion imaging
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Ventilation-perfusion imaging — Pulmonary embolism when CTPA is unsuitable
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Normal perfusion argues strongly against PE; a mismatched perfusion defect supports it.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pulmonary embolism when CTPA is unsuitable
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Provides an alternative when contrast, radiation distribution or renal considerations make CTPA unsuitable.

pathophysiology.summary: Venous thromboembolism results from venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. A deep-vein thrombus may obstruct limb venous return or embolise to pulmonary arteries, increasing dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance and, in severe cases, causing right-ventricular failure and shock.
keyMechanisms: Thrombus formation is promoted by immobility, surgery, cancer, oestrogen exposure, pregnancy and inherited or acquired thrombophilia.
Pulmonary arterial obstruction produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia.
Acute right-ventricular pressure overload can reduce left-ventricular filling and systemic cardiac output.
Residual venous obstruction and valve damage contribute to post-thrombotic syndrome; persistent vascular obstruction may cause chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

clinicalManagement.title: Estimate clinical probability
actions: Use a validated DVT or PE clinical-probability tool within its intended population.
Check haemodynamic stability and bleeding risk before selecting the diagnostic pathway.
Do not use a D-dimer to rule out VTE when clinical probability is high.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At first assessment

clinicalManagement.title: Obtain definitive imaging
actions: Arrange compression ultrasonography for suspected DVT and CTPA or appropriate ventilation-perfusion imaging for suspected PE.
Give interim therapeutic anticoagulation when indicated by the approved pathway and imaging is delayed, after checking contraindications.
Obtain baseline blood count, renal and liver function, coagulation studies and pregnancy testing when relevant without delaying urgent treatment.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently according to probability and stability

clinicalManagement.title: Start anticoagulation
actions: Select a locally formulary-approved anticoagulant based on renal and hepatic function, cancer, pregnancy potential, interactions, bleeding risk and patient preference.
Use generic agents and approved dosing references; do not derive dosing from this data record.
Document intended duration and the review point for extension or cessation.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Once VTE is confirmed or interim treatment is indicated

clinicalManagement.title: Manage high-risk pulmonary embolism
actions: Activate critical-care and senior specialist support for haemodynamic instability.
Consider systemic thrombolysis or another reperfusion strategy only after rapid assessment of contraindications and local capability.
Provide respiratory and circulatory support while definitive therapy is organised.
Seek urgent haematology or vascular advice.
Consider a temporary mechanical strategy only when guideline criteria are met, with an explicit retrieval plan.
branches.condition: Anticoagulation is contraindicated

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Plan secondary prevention
actions: Classify the event as provoked, unprovoked or cancer-associated and document persistent risk factors.
Review adherence, interactions and bleeding precautions.
Avoid routine thrombophilia testing when it will not change management; seek specialist advice for selected cases.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before discharge

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review early after discharge for symptoms, bleeding, adherence and renal function where relevant; reassess treatment duration at the guideline-defined milestone and investigate persistent dyspnoea for post-PE complications.
mdtReferrals: Haematology for recurrent, unusual-site or selected unprovoked VTE
Oncology for suspected or active cancer-associated thrombosis
Vascular or interventional service for threatened limb or selected reperfusion decisions
Obstetric medicine for pregnancy or postpartum VTE
lifestyleAndDiet: Encourage mobilisation as tolerated once anticoagulation and clinical stability permit.
Reduce prolonged immobility during travel and recovery and maintain hydration when appropriate.
Address smoking, obesity and other modifiable vascular risks without implying that lifestyle replaces anticoagulation.
patientEducation: Explain clot symptoms, anticoagulant purpose, adherence and what to do after a missed dose using the medicine-specific approved information.
Provide urgent warning signs for recurrent PE and major bleeding.
Discuss procedure, dental and pregnancy-planning precautions before any anticoagulant change.
dischargeCriteria: Haemodynamics and oxygenation are stable and validated outpatient-risk criteria are met where outpatient care is proposed.
Anticoagulant access, renal-function appropriateness, administration and follow-up are confirmed.
Bleeding and recurrence precautions are understood and a responsible service owns pending results.

content.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
content.specialty: Internal Medicine, Respiratory Medicine and Infectious Diseases

redFlags: Respiratory failure, exhaustion or rapidly increasing oxygen need
Shock, altered mental status, oliguria or other sepsis-associated organ dysfunction
Multilobar disease, cavitation or a large pleural effusion
Immunocompromise, aspiration risk or failure to improve on appropriate initial therapy
symptoms: Acute cough with or without sputum
Fever, rigors or malaise
Dyspnoea or pleuritic chest pain
Confusion or functional decline, especially in older adults
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, hypoxaemia or increased work of breathing
Focal crackles, bronchial breathing or dullness to percussion
Fever or hypothermia with tachycardia
Confusion, hypotension or poor perfusion in severe disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt pleuritic pain or dyspnoea, thrombosis risk and limited infective prodrome; imaging shows vascular rather than air-space disease.
Orthopnoea, bilateral congestion, raised jugular venous pressure and cardiac dysfunction.
Diffuse upper-respiratory features without focal consolidation or compatible chest imaging.
Subacute constitutional symptoms, epidemiologic risk, upper-lobe or cavitary change and specific microbiology.

ruleIn.testName: Chest radiograph
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph — Pulmonary air-space infection
ruleIn.expectedFinding: New focal or multifocal infiltrate compatible with pneumonia.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports diagnosis, extent assessment and detection of effusion or another thoracic process in hospital-managed disease.

ruleIn.testName: Pulse oximetry and blood gas when severe
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pulse oximetry and blood gas when severe — Gas-exchange impairment
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Hypoxaemia, with acidaemia or ventilatory failure in advanced disease.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines oxygen and ventilatory support needs.

ruleIn.testName: Microbiology selected by severity
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Microbiology selected by severity — Causative pathogen
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A plausible bacterial or viral pathogen in good-quality respiratory, blood or molecular samples.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Severe or epidemiologically important disease benefits most from organism identification and antimicrobial narrowing.

ruleOut.testName: Electrocardiogram and cardiac assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram and cardiac assessment — Heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No primary cardiac process sufficient to explain the presentation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Cardiac disease commonly mimics or coexists with pneumonia.

ruleOut.testName: CT chest or pleural ultrasound when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: CT chest or pleural ultrasound when indicated — Pulmonary embolism, malignancy, abscess or complicated effusion
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No alternative lesion, or a complication is identified for targeted management.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pulmonary embolism, malignancy, abscess or complicated effusion
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, complication assessment or treatment failure.

pathophysiology.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia is infection of the distal airways and alveoli acquired outside hospital or early after admission. Alveolar inflammation and exudate impair ventilation and gas exchange; systemic inflammatory effects may cause sepsis and organ dysfunction.
keyMechanisms: Pathogen aspiration or inhalation overcomes airway and innate immune defences.
Alveolar neutrophilic inflammation and fluid cause consolidation and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
Host response varies with age, comorbidity, immune status and pathogen virulence.
Complications include parapneumonic effusion, empyema, lung abscess, respiratory failure and sepsis.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and assess severity
actions: Assess oxygenation, sepsis features, comorbidity and ability to take oral treatment.
Use a validated severity tool as an adjunct, not a replacement for clinical judgement.
Identify aspiration, resistant-organism, travel and immunocompromise risks.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At presentation

clinicalManagement.title: Start empiric antimicrobial therapy
actions: Select generic therapy from the current MOH/local formulary according to severity, allergy, recent exposure and the local antibiogram.
Obtain indicated cultures first only when this will not delay urgent therapy.
Document indication, route, review date and planned duration.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly after diagnosis; immediately when sepsis or shock is present

clinicalManagement.title: Provide supportive care
actions: Titrate oxygen to the appropriate clinical target.
Treat sepsis, fluid deficit, pain and fever while accounting for cardiac and renal status.
Provide thrombosis prevention and early mobilisation for admitted patients when appropriate.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Concurrent with antimicrobial treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Review response and complications
actions: Reassess observations, oxygen need, mental status, oral intake and inflammatory/organ-function trends.
Narrow or change antimicrobials using microbiology and clinical response.
Investigate empyema, abscess, resistant pathogen, obstruction or an alternative diagnosis when improvement is absent.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Formal review within 24 to 48 hours or sooner if deteriorating

clinicalManagement.title: Switch route and plan discharge
actions: Switch from intravenous to oral treatment when stability and gastrointestinal absorption permit.
Use the shortest effective guideline-concordant course and document the stop date.
Arrange follow-up imaging only for persistent symptoms or guideline-defined risk, not automatically for every patient.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When clinically stable

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange clinical review based on severity and comorbidity; follow pending cultures, reassess non-resolution, and consider interval chest imaging for persistent symptoms or higher malignancy risk according to local policy.
mdtReferrals: Critical care for respiratory failure or shock
Respiratory medicine for complications, recurrent pneumonia or diagnostic uncertainty
Microbiology or infectious diseases for resistant organisms, severe immunocompromise or treatment failure
Speech and language therapy for suspected aspiration
lifestyleAndDiet: Encourage hydration and nutrition as tolerated.
Offer smoking-cessation support.
Review influenza, pneumococcal and other indicated vaccination after recovery.
patientEducation: Explain the expected recovery trajectory and that cough and fatigue may outlast fever.
Give return precautions for worsening breathlessness, confusion, cyanosis, chest pain or inability to maintain intake.
Explain antimicrobial adherence and why unused antibiotics should not be saved or shared.
dischargeCriteria: Vital signs and oxygen requirement are stable at an appropriate baseline.
The patient can take oral medicine and maintain hydration and nutrition.
A safe antimicrobial plan, follow-up ownership and return precautions are documented.

content.title: Breast Cancer Management
content.specialty: Medical Oncology, Breast Surgery and Radiation Oncology

redFlags: Rapidly progressive inflammatory breast change
Spinal pain with weakness, sensory change or bladder/bowel dysfunction
New focal neurological deficit, seizure or raised intracranial-pressure symptoms
Visceral crisis with organ dysfunction requiring rapid oncology assessment
symptoms: New breast or axillary lump
Nipple retraction or bloody discharge
Persistent focal breast change or skin dimpling
Bone pain, breathlessness, neurological symptoms or weight loss in advanced disease
physicalSigns: Discrete breast mass or asymmetric thickening
Peau d'orange, ulceration or inflammatory change
Nipple inversion or eczematous nipple lesion
Palpable axillary or supraclavicular nodes

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Often mobile, well-circumscribed and benign on age-appropriate imaging, but tissue diagnosis is required when assessment is discordant.
Fluid-filled lesion on ultrasound with resolution after aspiration in selected cases.
Pain, erythema, fever and a collection; non-resolution requires investigation for inflammatory malignancy.
History of trauma or surgery with characteristic imaging, although biopsy may be needed if suspicious.

ruleIn.testName: Triple assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Triple assessment — Breast malignancy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Concordant suspicious clinical examination, mammography/ultrasound and core-biopsy histology.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Integrates anatomy and tissue diagnosis while minimising false reassurance from any single test.

ruleIn.testName: Histopathology with ER, PR and HER2 testing
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Histopathology with ER, PR and HER2 testing — Invasive breast-cancer subtype
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Malignant morphology with grade and validated receptor status.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms diagnosis and directs endocrine, anti-HER2 and chemotherapy decisions.

ruleIn.testName: Stage-directed imaging
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Stage-directed imaging — Regional or distant metastatic disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Imaging defines tumour, nodal and metastatic burden when stage or symptoms justify it.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Avoids indiscriminate staging in low-risk disease while identifying treatment-changing metastases.

ruleOut.testName: Image-guided core biopsy of a suspicious benign-appearing lesion
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Image-guided core biopsy of a suspicious benign-appearing lesion — Benign breast disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Pathology is benign and concordant with clinical and imaging findings.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Discordance requires repeat sampling or excision rather than simple reassurance.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted imaging of new symptoms
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted imaging of new symptoms — Metastatic complication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No metastasis explaining the symptom, or a lesion is identified for urgent management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Routine surveillance imaging in asymptomatic early-stage survivors is not a substitute for symptom-led assessment.

pathophysiology.summary: Breast cancer comprises malignant epithelial tumours with heterogeneous hormone-receptor, HER2 and genomic biology. Disease may remain in situ, invade breast and regional lymphatics, or spread haematogenously to bone, liver, lung and brain; biology and stage jointly determine treatment and prognosis.
keyMechanisms: Accumulated genomic and epigenetic alterations enable uncontrolled proliferation and invasion.
Oestrogen/progesterone-receptor signalling and HER2 amplification define actionable biological subsets.
Lymphatic spread commonly involves axillary and regional nodes.
Tumour heterogeneity and treatment selection pressure can change receptor status in recurrent disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm pathology and stage
actions: Obtain adequate core tissue and report histological type, grade and ER, PR and HER2 status.
Complete stage-appropriate imaging and assess performance status, comorbidities and baseline organ function.
Arrange genetic and fertility counselling when clinical criteria are met.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before definitive treatment

clinicalManagement.title: Agree a multidisciplinary plan
actions: Discuss every new case in a breast multidisciplinary conference.
Integrate stage, biology, patient goals, surgical feasibility and treatment toxicities.
Record sequence of surgery, systemic therapy and radiotherapy with responsible teams.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After diagnostic work-up

clinicalManagement.title: Deliver local-regional therapy
actions: Offer breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy according to disease extent, contraindications and informed preference.
Stage the axilla using the appropriate sentinel-node or nodal procedure.
Plan radiotherapy according to surgical approach, margins, nodal involvement and recurrence risk.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to stage and treatment sequence

clinicalManagement.title: Select biology-directed systemic therapy
actions: Use endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive disease when indicated.
Use generic anti-HER2 therapy for eligible HER2-positive disease with cardiac monitoring.
Select chemotherapy and any contemporary targeted or immunotherapy only through the current approved oncology protocol.
Prioritise neoadjuvant systemic therapy and serial response assessment.
Proceed to local therapy if disease becomes operable and the MDT confirms benefit.
branches.condition: Locally advanced or inflammatory disease

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Neoadjuvant or adjuvant as agreed by MDT

clinicalManagement.title: Survivorship or advanced-disease review
actions: Use interval history, examination and mammography of retained breast tissue according to policy.
Manage endocrine, bone, cardiac, menopausal and lymphoedema effects.
For metastatic disease, prioritise symptom control, quality of life and biology-directed therapy with early supportive care.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After initial treatment and throughout follow-up

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow the current Saudi oncology surveillance schedule, including clinical review and mammography where breast tissue remains; monitor therapy-specific cardiac, bone, gynaecological and lymphoedema risks and investigate new symptoms promptly.
mdtReferrals: Breast surgeon, medical oncologist, radiation oncologist and breast-care nurse
Genetics for hereditary-risk criteria
Fertility service before gonadotoxic treatment when relevant
Physiotherapy/lymphoedema, psycho-oncology and palliative care according to need
lifestyleAndDiet: Support regular physical activity and maintenance of a healthy body composition during and after treatment.
Provide dietetic advice for treatment-related weight change, nausea or malnutrition.
Offer smoking-cessation support and advise avoidance of unreviewed supplements that may interact with therapy.
patientEducation: Explain stage, receptor status, treatment intent and the role of each modality in plain language.
Discuss expected adverse effects, fertility, sexual health, pregnancy considerations and when to seek urgent care.
Provide individualised information on recurrence symptoms without encouraging harmful routine self-testing.
dischargeCriteria: The diagnosis, stage, receptor profile and MDT plan are documented.
Acute treatment complications are controlled and the patient has clear contacts.
Surveillance ownership, medicine monitoring and urgent symptom pathways are explicit.

content.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome Assessment and Escalation Pathway

redFlags: Persistent or recurrent suspected cardiac chest discomfort
Acute ischaemic ECG pattern
Syncope, shock, pulmonary oedema, or life-threatening arrhythmia
Cardiac arrest or new neurological deficit
symptoms: Chest pressure, tightness, heaviness, or discomfort
Discomfort radiating to arm, shoulder, jaw, back, or upper abdomen
Dyspnoea, nausea, sweating, or unusual fatigue
Atypical or minimal symptoms, especially in older adults and people with diabetes
physicalSigns: Pallor, diaphoresis, or respiratory distress
Tachycardia, bradycardia, hypotension, or irregular pulse
Possible heart-failure signs such as crackles or raised jugular venous pressure

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Abrupt severe chest or back pain, pulse or blood-pressure asymmetry, or new aortic regurgitation.
Acute dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, hypoxaemia, or venous thromboembolism risk factors.
Often pleuritic or positional pain with compatible ECG findings.
May be meal-related, reflux-associated, movement-related, or reproducible; these features alone do not exclude ACS.

ruleIn.testName: 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Acute myocardial ischaemia or infarction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: ST elevation or depression, dynamic T-wave change, or another acute ischaemic pattern
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identify immediately actionable ischaemia and guide escalation.

ruleIn.testName: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin — Acute myocardial injury
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Rise or fall with at least one value above the assay-specific 99th percentile, interpreted with symptoms and ECG
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detect myocardial injury using symptom timing and the local assay pathway.

ruleIn.testName: Bedside echocardiography when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Bedside echocardiography when indicated — Regional ventricular dysfunction or mechanical complication
ruleIn.expectedFinding: New regional wall-motion abnormality or cardiac dysfunction
ruleIn.targetCondition: Regional ventricular dysfunction or mechanical complication
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess instability or complications when clinically indicated.

ruleOut.testName: Serial 12-lead electrocardiograms
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serial 12-lead electrocardiograms — Evolving acute myocardial ischaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No dynamic ischaemic changes during assessment
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Repeat ECG when symptoms persist or recur; one normal ECG does not exclude ACS.

ruleOut.testName: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin using a validated local pathway
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin using a validated local pathway — Acute myocardial infarction
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Values and change below pathway rule-out thresholds with appropriate timing
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Support rule-out only when the complete validated pathway and clinical assessment permit.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph when indicated — Selected alternative acute thoracic causes
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No finding supporting an alternative such as pulmonary oedema or pneumothorax
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assess relevant alternatives; a normal result does not rule out ACS.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute myocardial ischaemia usually results from reduced coronary blood flow and may progress to infarction, arrhythmia, or haemodynamic compromise.
keyMechanisms: Atherosclerotic plaque disruption with platelet activation and thrombosis
Reduced myocardial oxygen supply relative to demand
Progressive myocardial injury

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate assessment and stabilisation
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, vital signs, and pain.
Obtain and interpret a 12-lead ECG promptly; repeat for persistent or changing symptoms.
Monitor and establish access according to acuity and local protocol.
Take focused history including onset, risk factors, medicines, allergies, and bleeding risk.
Activate local emergency, cardiology, and reperfusion pathways when indicated.
Begin the relevant resuscitation or emergency stabilisation pathway.
Request immediate senior, critical-care, and cardiology support.
Do not delay escalation for routine investigations.
branches.condition: Arrest, shock, life-threatening arrhythmia, or pulmonary oedema

actions: Escalate urgently for senior assessment and targeted evaluation.
Assess competing diagnoses and contraindications before ACS-directed treatment.
branches.condition: Aortic dissection or another time-critical alternative is suspected

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm working diagnosis and risk
actions: Use serial ECG and biomarker testing under the local validated pathway.
Order blood count, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, and other tests as indicated.
Assess haemodynamic status, bleeding risk, comorbidities, and suitability for invasive or reperfusion strategies.
Document diagnostic uncertainty and escalation plan.
Activate the local reperfusion pathway without waiting for routine serial biomarkers.
Arrange urgent transfer if required by local capability.
branches.condition: ECG or clinical status indicates immediate reperfusion

actions: Continue observation and serial ECG and biomarker assessment.
Escalate for recurrent pain, ECG changes, or deterioration.
branches.condition: Initial ECG is non-diagnostic but ACS remains possible

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Initial emergency assessment

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition and prevention planning
actions: Admit or transfer confirmed ACS, high-risk cases, or unresolved diagnostic concern.
Use the approved ACS protocol and specialist input for treatment decisions.
For discharged patients, document stability, follow-up, and return precautions.
Arrange cardiology and cardiac-rehabilitation follow-up after confirmed ACS.
Continue monitored hospital care and specialist-led management.
Document receiving team and structured handover.
branches.condition: ACS confirmed or high-risk features persist

actions: Provide a documented explanation and follow-up plan.
Advise emergency reassessment for recurrent or worsening symptoms.
branches.condition: ACS excluded through local pathway and no emergency alternative suspected

clinicalManagement.timeframe: After initial risk assessment

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange follow-up for the final diagnosis; confirmed ACS requires a documented cardiology and cardiac-rehabilitation plan.
mdtReferrals: Emergency medicine
Cardiology
Critical care when indicated
Cardiac rehabilitation
Primary care
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer individualised tobacco-cessation support, heart-healthy eating, physical activity, and cardiovascular risk reduction after acute assessment.
patientEducation: Explain urgent ECGs, blood tests, monitoring, and possible transfer.
Discuss warning symptoms requiring emergency reassessment.
For confirmed ACS, explain follow-up and prescribed risk-reduction plan.
dischargeCriteria: Time-critical causes have been assessed using an appropriate pathway.
Patient is clinically stable and disposition is documented.
Follow-up instructions and return precautions are communicated.

content.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Longitudinal Care Pathway

redFlags: Altered mental status, severe dehydration, or inability to maintain intake
Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, or suspected metabolic crisis
Severe hypoglycaemia or infected, ischaemic, or ulcerated foot
symptoms: May be asymptomatic and found on screening
Increased thirst, urination, or hunger
Fatigue, blurred vision, recurrent infections, or unintentional weight change
physicalSigns: Central adiposity or other metabolic risk features
Acanthosis nigricans in some patients
Possible peripheral sensory loss, foot lesions, or vascular disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May have rapid onset, ketosis, or insulin deficiency; investigate classification when uncertain.
Temporal association with glucocorticoids or other glucose-affecting medicines.
Pancreatic disease, endocrinopathy, or another underlying cause suggested by history or course.
Occurs during acute illness and may resolve; confirm persistent diabetes when appropriate.

ruleIn.testName: Laboratory HbA1c
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Laboratory HbA1c — Chronic hyperglycaemia consistent with diabetes
ruleIn.expectedFinding: At or above locally adopted diagnostic threshold, confirmed as required
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Estimate average glycaemia when assay and patient factors permit.

ruleIn.testName: Fasting plasma glucose
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Fasting plasma glucose — Diabetes mellitus
ruleIn.expectedFinding: At or above locally adopted diagnostic threshold, confirmed as required
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess fasting glycaemia using laboratory criteria.

ruleIn.testName: Random plasma glucose with classic symptoms or crisis
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Random plasma glucose with classic symptoms or crisis — Diabetes mellitus
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Marked hyperglycaemia meeting accepted criteria in the clinical context
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: May establish diagnosis in symptomatic patients while acute status is assessed.

ruleIn.testName: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and estimated glomerular filtration rate
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and estimated glomerular filtration rate — Diabetic kidney disease risk
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Albuminuria and/or reduced estimated filtration
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identify kidney involvement and inform risk and treatment planning.

ruleOut.testName: Repeat laboratory HbA1c or plasma glucose
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Repeat laboratory HbA1c or plasma glucose — Persistent diabetes after borderline or discordant result
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Repeat result below diagnostic thresholds without other diagnostic evidence
ruleOut.targetCondition: Persistent diabetes after borderline or discordant result
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Resolve uncertain results and consider factors affecting HbA1c.

ruleOut.testName: Blood ketones, electrolytes, renal function, and acid-base assessment when acutely unwell
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Blood ketones, electrolytes, renal function, and acid-base assessment when acutely unwell — Diabetic ketoacidosis or acute metabolic emergency
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No significant ketonaemia, acidosis, or related derangement
ruleOut.targetCondition: Diabetic ketoacidosis or acute metabolic emergency
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Assess an acute emergency when symptoms suggest it.

ruleOut.testName: Lipid profile and cardiovascular risk assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Lipid profile and cardiovascular risk assessment — Associated cardiovascular risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Risk profile characterised for management
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: These assess associated risk rather than exclude diabetes.

pathophysiology.summary: Type 2 diabetes is chronic hyperglycaemia associated with insulin resistance and progressive impairment of insulin secretion, with risk of vascular and other complications.
keyMechanisms: Reduced insulin sensitivity in liver, muscle, and adipose tissue
Progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction
Chronic hyperglycaemia contributing to microvascular and macrovascular injury

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and baseline risk
actions: Confirm diabetes using accepted laboratory criteria and repeat when required.
Review symptoms, medicines, pregnancy potential, cardiovascular history, and patient priorities.
Assess blood pressure, weight, smoking, lipids, kidney health, and feet.
Arrange complication screening under local guidance.
Arrange urgent specialist assessment and evaluate acute metabolic status.
Do not delay necessary treatment while classification is clarified.
branches.condition: Possible type 1 diabetes, ketosis, or rapid deterioration

actions: Arrange emergency assessment.
Use the local acute hyperglycaemia protocol.
branches.condition: Hyperglycaemic crisis or severe dehydration suspected

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis or transfer of care

clinicalManagement.title: Agree an individualised management plan
actions: Agree glycaemic and cardiovascular goals with the patient.
Offer structured education, nutrition support, activity advice, and tobacco cessation.
Select glucose-lowering therapy using current local guidance, comorbidities, renal function, contraindications, and preference.
Review response, adverse effects, adherence barriers, and hypoglycaemia risk.
Consider therapies with relevant outcome benefits under current local guidance and eligibility.
Coordinate with relevant specialists.
branches.condition: Cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease

actions: Arrange prompt preconception or obstetric-diabetes review.
Review medicines for pregnancy suitability with the specialist team.
branches.condition: Pregnant, planning pregnancy, or pregnancy possible

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis and reviewed regularly

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor complications and revise care
actions: Monitor glycaemia and treatment safety at an appropriate interval.
Review kidney function, urine albumin, blood pressure, lipids, feet, eyes, and cardiovascular risk.
Provide medicine-specific sick-day advice under local guidance.
Escalate persistent poor control, recurrent hypoglycaemia, or progressive complications.
Arrange timely foot-team or vascular assessment based on severity.
Use an urgent pathway for infection or threatened limb.
branches.condition: Foot ulcer, infection, ischaemia, or new sensory loss

actions: Review diagnosis, adherence barriers, tolerance, and social context.
Adjust treatment or refer according to local guidance.
branches.condition: Targets unmet or complications progressing

clinicalManagement.timeframe: At least annually and more often when indicated

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review glycaemia, medicines, cardiovascular risk, kidneys, eyes, and feet regularly; increase review frequency after treatment changes or when control requires closer monitoring.
mdtReferrals: Diabetes educator or nurse
Dietitian
Retinal screening service
Foot-care service
Endocrinology when indicated
Nephrology, cardiology, or vascular service when indicated
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer culturally appropriate nutrition counselling and sustainable goals.
Encourage regular activity adapted to ability and health.
Offer support for weight management, sleep, and tobacco cessation where relevant.
patientEducation: Explain diabetes, monitoring, treatment choices, and when to seek urgent help.
Provide accessible self-management education in the preferred language.
Discuss foot care and regular eye, kidney, and cardiovascular checks.
dischargeCriteria: Patient is clinically stable with an agreed self-management and follow-up plan.
Acute metabolic emergencies and limb-threatening complications are addressed.
Patient knows how to access help and seek urgent review.

content.title: Adult Essential Hypertension Screening and Confirmation

redFlags: Severe elevation with chest pain, dyspnoea, neurological deficit, confusion, visual loss, or acute kidney injury
Pregnancy with elevated pressure or pre-eclampsia symptoms
Abrupt onset, resistant readings, or suspected secondary cause
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic
Occasional non-specific headache or dizziness, which cannot establish diagnosis
physicalSigns: Elevated pressure on correctly performed measurement
Possible target-organ disease in established hypertension
Possible clinical clues to a secondary cause

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Clinic readings elevated but validated out-of-office average not persistently elevated.
Clinic readings may be below threshold while home or ambulatory readings are elevated.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistance, relevant medicines, renal or endocrine clues.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness, stimulants, or measurement error; repeat under standardised conditions.

ruleIn.testName: Repeated standardised clinic blood-pressure measurement
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Repeated standardised clinic blood-pressure measurement — Persistently elevated blood pressure
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Repeated readings meeting locally adopted threshold using validated device and correct cuff
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Reduce misclassification from poor technique or transient elevation.

ruleIn.testName: Home or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Out-of-office average meeting locally adopted threshold
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirm persistence and identify white-coat or masked hypertension.

ruleIn.testName: Creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, electrolytes, urine albumin, and urinalysis
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, electrolytes, urine albumin, and urinalysis — Target-organ involvement or possible secondary hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Renal impairment, albuminuria, electrolyte abnormality, or other finding needing assessment
ruleIn.targetCondition: Target-organ involvement or possible secondary hypertension
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess baseline kidney health and direct further evaluation.

ruleIn.testName: Electrocardiogram
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram — Cardiac target-organ involvement
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Possible left ventricular hypertrophy, rhythm abnormality, or prior cardiac disease
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess cardiovascular context; normal ECG does not exclude hypertension.

ruleOut.testName: Repeat standardised readings after rest
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Repeat standardised readings after rest — Transient or measurement-related elevation
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Repeat readings below locally adopted threshold
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Check for technique-related or transient elevation.

ruleOut.testName: Validated home or ambulatory monitoring
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Validated home or ambulatory monitoring — White-coat hypertension
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Out-of-office average below local threshold despite elevated clinic readings
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoid relying on clinic readings alone when results are discordant.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted secondary-hypertension investigations
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted secondary-hypertension investigations — Secondary cause of elevated blood pressure
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No targeted evidence for the suspected cause
ruleOut.targetCondition: Secondary cause of elevated blood pressure
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Select testing using clinical indications rather than broad routine testing.

pathophysiology.summary: Essential hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure without an identified secondary cause. It is often asymptomatic and increases cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and kidney risk.
keyMechanisms: Interactions among genetic, renal, vascular, neurohormonal, and environmental factors
Increased systemic vascular resistance and altered sodium-volume regulation
Cumulative pressure-related vascular and target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.title: Screen and measure accurately
actions: Use a validated device, correct cuff, and standardised seated measurement after rest.
Obtain repeat readings and document method, values, symptoms, and context.
Review medicines, supplements, stimulants, tobacco, pain, and acute illness.
Do not diagnose from one isolated value unless urgent circumstances require action.
Arrange repeat and out-of-office confirmation within a risk-appropriate interval.
Explain follow-up and symptoms needing urgent assessment.
branches.condition: Elevated screening measurement without acute symptoms

actions: Arrange immediate emergency assessment.
Avoid rapid unsupervised outpatient lowering.
branches.condition: Severe elevation with possible acute target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Preventive and primary-care encounters, or when indicated

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and assess risk
actions: Confirm sustained hypertension with repeated clinic and/or validated out-of-office readings.
Assess cardiovascular risk, kidney function, diabetes, lipids, smoking, and target-organ injury.
Investigate secondary causes when clinical indications are present.
Agree an individualised plan and follow-up interval.
Consider white-coat hypertension rather than labelling sustained disease.
Continue monitoring based on overall risk.
branches.condition: Out-of-office values are not persistently elevated

actions: Arrange targeted work-up and specialist input as appropriate.
Address urgent complications through emergency care.
branches.condition: Secondary cause or target-organ injury suspected

clinicalManagement.timeframe: After elevated screening readings

clinicalManagement.title: Reduce risk and provide ongoing care
actions: Offer lifestyle measures and treatment options under current local guidance.
Select medication when indicated based on comorbidities, renal function, pregnancy potential, contraindications, and preference.
Review pressure, adherence, adverse effects, renal function, and risk after treatment changes.
Escalate persistent uncontrolled readings or suspected complications.
Use a pregnancy-specific assessment and treatment pathway.
Review medicines promptly and involve obstetric care when indicated.
branches.condition: Pregnancy or pregnancy potential

actions: Confirm measurement technique and adherence; review interfering medicines and secondary causes.
Adjust treatment or refer under local guidance.
branches.condition: Pressure remains above agreed target

clinicalManagement.timeframe: After diagnosis and at regular follow-up

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange repeat clinic or out-of-office measurements and cardiovascular-risk review according to results, patient risk, and local guidance.
mdtReferrals: Primary care or family medicine
Dietitian or lifestyle support
Cardiology, nephrology, or endocrinology when indicated
Obstetrics for pregnancy-associated hypertension
lifestyleAndDiet: Discuss balanced eating and sodium reduction where appropriate.
Encourage regular activity, healthy weight goals, and tobacco cessation.
Discuss alcohol use consistent with health needs and local advice.
patientEducation: Explain that hypertension is often symptom-free and needs accurate measurement and follow-up.
Teach home-monitoring technique when used.
Explain urgent symptoms requiring immediate assessment.
dischargeCriteria: Measurement result, confirmation plan, and precautions are documented.
Acute target-organ injury is assessed and disposition determined.
Patient knows when blood pressure will be reassessed.

redFlags: Fever, persistent pain, or systemic illness
Jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, or suspected duct obstruction
Severe persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back
Pregnancy, anticoagulation, or significant cardiopulmonary instability requiring modified planning
symptoms: Episodic right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain, sometimes after meals
Possible nausea or vomiting during biliary colic
Known symptomatic gallstones with a documented surgical plan
physicalSigns: Often normal between episodes
Possible right-upper-quadrant tenderness
Jaundice, fever, or marked tenderness suggests complication and needs reassessment

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Persistent right-upper-quadrant pain and tenderness, often with fever or inflammatory findings.
Jaundice or cholestatic laboratory pattern; fever and systemic illness raise concern for cholangitis.

pathophysiology.summary:
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) describes an acute spectrum of myocardial ischaemia caused by an abrupt imbalance between oxygen supply and myocardial demand. A common initiating event is disruption or erosion of an atherosclerotic coronary plaque. Exposure of thrombogenic material activates platelets and the coagulation cascade, producing a thrombus that may partially or completely obstruct coronary flow. Vasoconstriction, distal microembolisation, and pre-existing fixed stenoses can further reduce perfusion. Less commonly, coronary spasm, spontaneous dissection, embolism, or severe supply–demand mismatch produces an ACS-like presentation without acute plaque thrombosis.

The amount and duration of flow reduction, collateral circulation, and myocardial oxygen demand determine whether injury remains transient or progresses to irreversible necrosis. Ischaemic myocardium develops electrical instability and impaired contractility; this can cause dynamic ECG changes, ventricular dysfunction, acute heart failure, shock, or malignant arrhythmia. When cardiomyocyte injury occurs, intracellular proteins including cardiac troponin enter the circulation. A rise or fall in troponin indicates acute myocardial injury, but infarction requires interpretation alongside evidence of ischaemia such as symptoms, ECG findings, imaging, or coronary thrombus. Therefore, ACS is not defined by a single symptom, ECG, or biomarker result. The clinical spectrum includes unstable angina and myocardial infarction with or without persistent ST elevation; the pattern reflects the severity and persistence of ischaemia and the presence of myocardial necrosis. Older adults, women, and people with diabetes may have less typical symptoms, so assessment integrates the history, serial ECGs, assay-specific troponin pathways, haemodynamic state, and competing time-critical diagnoses. This explanation is an educational synthesis; classification and treatment decisions must follow current local protocols and specialist assessment.

keyMechanisms: Atherosclerotic plaque disruption or erosion with platelet activation and thrombus formation

pathophysiology.summary: Lung cancer arises from malignant transformation of respiratory epithelium and is broadly classified as non-small-cell or small-cell carcinoma. Local invasion, lymphatic spread and early haematogenous dissemination determine resectability and systemic treatment; molecular drivers and immune phenotype increasingly guide therapy.
keyMechanisms: Tobacco smoke, environmental and occupational carcinogens produce cumulative genomic injury.
Histological subtype and molecular alterations determine growth pattern and treatment sensitivity.
Mediastinal nodal involvement strongly affects stage and curative options.
Metastatic spread commonly affects brain, bone, liver and adrenal glands; paraneoplastic syndromes may precede local symptoms.
