redFlags: Ongoing heavy bleeding or shock
Altered consciousness or collapse
Coagulopathy or rapidly falling haemoglobin
Suspected uterine rupture or retained placenta
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Postpartum Haemorrhage Response, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Inspect for lacerations when appropriate.
Assess placenta and uterine cavity per protocol.

ruleIn.testName: Quantified blood loss and serial maternal observations
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Quantified blood loss and serial maternal observations — Ongoing haemorrhage and circulatory compromise
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Continuing blood loss, tachycardia or falling pressure raises concern; physiological change may lag behind bleeding.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Tracks severity and response while resuscitation and cause control proceed.

ruleIn.testName: Full blood count, coagulation and fibrinogen
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Full blood count, coagulation and fibrinogen — Anaemia, platelet deficiency and coagulopathy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Falling haemoglobin/platelets or abnormal coagulation/fibrinogen informs blood-product assessment; early haemoglobin can be misleading.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Guides the haemorrhage/transfusion pathway without delaying immediate treatment.

ruleIn.testName: Blood group and crossmatch
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood group and crossmatch — Compatible blood products
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Compatibility testing enables appropriate transfusion support.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Prepares urgently needed products through the local major-haemorrhage protocol.

ruleOut.testName: Focused obstetric examination with ultrasound when useful
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Focused obstetric examination with ultrasound when useful — Atony, trauma, retained tissue or another bleeding cause
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Uterine tone, genital trauma or retained tissue directs cause-specific intervention.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Atony, trauma, retained tissue or another bleeding cause
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies the source; imaging must not delay action for clinically evident haemorrhage.

pathophysiology.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage results from impaired uterine contraction, genital tract trauma, retained tissue, or coagulation failure. redFlags: Severe hypoxemia (SpO2 < 88% on oxygen).
Acute respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35 with PaCO2 > 45 mmHg).
Altered mental status, confusion, or lethargy (indicating CO2 narcosis).
symptoms: Acute worsening of dyspnea (out of proportion to day-to-day variation).
Increased sputum volume.
Increased sputum purulence.
physicalSigns: Tachypnea (>25 breaths/min), use of accessory muscles, and paradoxical abdominal movement indicating impending fatigue.
Widespread wheeze, decreased breath sounds, and prolonged expiratory phase.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Focal consolidation on chest X-ray, significant fever, and localized crackles rather than generalized wheeze.
Bilateral basal crackles, elevated JVP, cardiomegaly or pleural effusions on X-ray, and elevated BNP.
Consider if dyspnea onset is sudden and pleuritic, with an absence of increased sputum purulence, accompanied by tachycardia or right heart strain on ECG.

clinicalManagement.title: Step 1: Oxygenation Target
actions: Administer controlled oxygen via Venturi mask.
Strict Target: SpO2 88–92%. Do not over-oxygenate due to the risk of worsening V/Q mismatch and hypercapnia.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediate

clinicalManagement.title: Step 2: Pharmacological Interventions
actions: Bronchodilators: Salbutamol 2.5–5 mg nebulized + Ipratropium 500 mcg nebulized every 1–4 hours as needed.
Systemic Corticosteroids: Prednisolone 40 mg PO daily for 5 days. (Use IV Hydrocortisone only if patient is unable to take oral medication).

Antibiotics: Indicated ONLY if all 3 cardinal symptoms are present, OR if 2 are present (one being increased purulence), OR if requiring mechanical ventilation. Give Azithromycin or Doxycycline for 5–7 days.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Start promptly and reassess

pathophysiology.summary: An acute exacerbation is a sustained worsening of airflow obstruction caused by bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, airway-wall oedema and mucus plugging on a background of variable airway inflammation. Severe obstruction raises the work of breathing, produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and may progress from hypocapnia to carbon-dioxide retention as respiratory muscles fatigue.
keyMechanisms: Trigger-driven airway inflammation and bronchial hyper-responsiveness narrow conducting airways.
Mucosal oedema and tenacious secretions amplify expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation.
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; a normalising or rising carbon dioxide level in a distressed patient can indicate fatigue.
Prolonged expiration and air trapping increase intrathoracic pressure and the work of breathing.

pathophysiology.summary: An acute exacerbation is a sustained worsening of airflow obstruction caused by bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, airway-wall oedema and mucus plugging on a background of variable airway inflammation. Severe obstruction raises the work of breathing, produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and may progress from hypocapnia to carbon-dioxide retention as respiratory muscles fatigue.
keyMechanisms: Trigger-driven airway inflammation and bronchial hyper-responsiveness narrow conducting airways.
Mucosal oedema and tenacious secretions amplify expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation.
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; a normalising or rising carbon dioxide level in a distressed patient can indicate fatigue.
Prolonged expiration and air trapping increase intrathoracic pressure and the work of breathing.

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate assessment and stabilisation
actions: Use an airway-breathing-circulation approach and call senior emergency support for severe or life-threatening features.
Position upright when tolerated, establish monitoring and obtain intravenous access without delaying inhaled therapy.
Give controlled oxygen to the locally approved saturation target and reassess frequently.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately on arrival

clinicalManagement.title: Reverse bronchoconstriction
actions: Give repeated inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist using an appropriate delivery system.
Add inhaled ipratropium bromide in severe or life-threatening exacerbation.
Document response using symptoms, respiratory effort, oxygenation and peak flow where feasible.
Escalate immediately to a senior emergency/critical-care clinician.
Consider continuous nebulised bronchodilator delivery and intravenous magnesium sulfate under the approved local protocol.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat airway inflammation
actions: Administer systemic corticosteroid promptly unless contraindicated.
Review likely trigger, adherence and recent corticosteroid exposure.
Do not use antibiotics routinely unless bacterial infection is clinically supported.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Early in the first hour

clinicalManagement.title: Structured reassessment
actions: Repeat respiratory rate, work of breathing, speech, oxygen saturation and peak flow where possible.
Check for complications and alternative diagnoses if the trajectory is not improving.
Escalate for ventilatory support planning before exhaustion or reduced consciousness develops.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After each initial treatment cycle

actions: Admit patients with persistent severe features, oxygen requirement, poor social support or high relapse risk.
Before discharge, verify inhaler technique, provide an individualised written action plan and arrange controller therapy review.
Explain explicit emergency return precautions.

content.title: Adult Essential Hypertension Screening and Confirmation

redFlags: Severe elevation with chest pain, dyspnoea, neurological deficit, confusion, visual loss, or acute kidney injury
Pregnancy with elevated pressure or pre-eclampsia symptoms
Abrupt onset, resistant readings, or suspected secondary cause
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic
Occasional non-specific headache or dizziness, which cannot establish diagnosis
physicalSigns: Elevated pressure on correctly performed measurement
Possible target-organ disease in established hypertension
Possible clinical clues to a secondary cause

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Clinic readings elevated but validated out-of-office average not persistently elevated.
Clinic readings may be below threshold while home or ambulatory readings are elevated.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistance, relevant medicines, renal or endocrine clues.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness, stimulants, or measurement error; repeat under standardised conditions.

ruleIn.testName: Repeated standardised clinic blood-pressure measurement
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Repeated standardised clinic blood-pressure measurement — Persistently elevated blood pressure
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Repeated readings meeting locally adopted threshold using validated device and correct cuff
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Reduce misclassification from poor technique or transient elevation.

ruleIn.testName: Home or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Out-of-office average meeting locally adopted threshold
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirm persistence and identify white-coat or masked hypertension.

ruleIn.testName: Creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, electrolytes, urine albumin, and urinalysis
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, electrolytes, urine albumin, and urinalysis — Target-organ involvement or possible secondary hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Renal impairment, albuminuria, electrolyte abnormality, or other finding needing assessment
ruleIn.targetCondition: Target-organ involvement or possible secondary hypertension
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess baseline kidney health and direct further evaluation.

ruleIn.testName: Electrocardiogram
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram — Cardiac target-organ involvement
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Possible left ventricular hypertrophy, rhythm abnormality, or prior cardiac disease
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assess cardiovascular context; normal ECG does not exclude hypertension.

ruleOut.testName: Repeat standardised readings after rest
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Repeat standardised readings after rest — Transient or measurement-related elevation
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Repeat readings below locally adopted threshold
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Check for technique-related or transient elevation.

ruleOut.testName: Validated home or ambulatory monitoring
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Validated home or ambulatory monitoring — White-coat hypertension
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Out-of-office average below local threshold despite elevated clinic readings
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Avoid relying on clinic readings alone when results are discordant.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted secondary-hypertension investigations
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted secondary-hypertension investigations — Secondary cause of elevated blood pressure
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No targeted evidence for the suspected cause
ruleOut.targetCondition: Secondary cause of elevated blood pressure
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Select testing using clinical indications rather than broad routine testing.

steps.test: Standardised clinic blood pressure in both arms

steps.decision_rationale: NICE specifies standardised technique, repeat measurement and bilateral assessment.

steps.test: Ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring
steps.timeframe: After raised clinic blood pressure is identified

steps.clinical_question: Is hypertension confirmed outside the clinic?
steps.decision_rationale: NICE recommends ABPM, or HBPM when ABPM is unsuitable, for confirmation below severe-hypertension thresholds.

steps.test: Target-organ-damage assessment
steps.expected_finding: Urine ACR and haematuria testing, HbA1c, electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, cholesterol, fundoscopy and 12-lead ECG identify associated risk or damage.
steps.clinical_question: Is there renal, metabolic, retinal or cardiac involvement?
steps.decision_rationale: NICE recommends this assessment for all people with hypertension.

pathophysiology.summary: Essential hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure without an identified secondary cause. It is often asymptomatic and increases cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and kidney risk.
keyMechanisms: Interactions among genetic, renal, vascular, neurohormonal, and environmental factors
Increased systemic vascular resistance and altered sodium-volume regulation
Cumulative pressure-related vascular and target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.title: Screen and measure accurately
actions: Use a validated device, correct cuff, and standardised seated measurement after rest.
Obtain repeat readings and document method, values, symptoms, and context.
Review medicines, supplements, stimulants, tobacco, pain, and acute illness.
Do not diagnose from one isolated value unless urgent circumstances require action.
Arrange repeat and out-of-office confirmation within a risk-appropriate interval.
Explain follow-up and symptoms needing urgent assessment.
branches.condition: Elevated screening measurement without acute symptoms

actions: Arrange immediate emergency assessment.
Avoid rapid unsupervised outpatient lowering.
branches.condition: Severe elevation with possible acute target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Preventive and primary-care encounters, or when indicated

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and assess risk
actions: Confirm sustained hypertension with repeated clinic and/or validated out-of-office readings.
Assess cardiovascular risk, kidney function, diabetes, lipids, smoking, and target-organ injury.
Investigate secondary causes when clinical indications are present.
Agree an individualised plan and follow-up interval.
Consider white-coat hypertension rather than labelling sustained disease.
Continue monitoring based on overall risk.
branches.condition: Out-of-office values are not persistently elevated

actions: Arrange targeted work-up and specialist input as appropriate.
Address urgent complications through emergency care.
branches.condition: Secondary cause or target-organ injury suspected

clinicalManagement.timeframe: After elevated screening readings

clinicalManagement.title: Reduce risk and provide ongoing care
actions: Offer lifestyle measures and treatment options under current local guidance.
Select medication when indicated based on comorbidities, renal function, pregnancy potential, contraindications, and preference.
Review pressure, adherence, adverse effects, renal function, and risk after treatment changes.
Escalate persistent uncontrolled readings or suspected complications.
Use a pregnancy-specific assessment and treatment pathway.
Review medicines promptly and involve obstetric care when indicated.
branches.condition: Pregnancy or pregnancy potential

actions: Confirm measurement technique and adherence; review interfering medicines and secondary causes.
Adjust treatment or refer under local guidance.
branches.condition: Pressure remains above agreed target

clinicalManagement.timeframe: After diagnosis and at regular follow-up

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange repeat clinic or out-of-office measurements and cardiovascular-risk review according to results, patient risk, and local guidance.
mdtReferrals: Primary care or family medicine
Dietitian or lifestyle support
Cardiology, nephrology, or endocrinology when indicated
Obstetrics for pregnancy-associated hypertension
lifestyleAndDiet: Discuss balanced eating and sodium reduction where appropriate.
Encourage regular activity, healthy weight goals, and tobacco cessation.
Discuss alcohol use consistent with health needs and local advice.
patientEducation: Explain that hypertension is often symptom-free and needs accurate measurement and follow-up.
Teach home-monitoring technique when used.
Explain urgent symptoms requiring immediate assessment.
dischargeCriteria: Measurement result, confirmation plan, and precautions are documented.
Acute target-organ injury is assessed and disposition determined.
Patient knows when blood pressure will be reassessed.

redFlags: Chest pain, focal neurological deficit, severe breathlessness or syncope discovered during screening
Markedly elevated blood pressure with acute target-organ symptoms
Suicidal ideation or immediate safeguarding concern
Alarm cancer symptoms such as unexplained bleeding, persistent mass or major unintentional weight loss
symptoms: Often asymptomatic attendance for preventive review
May disclose fatigue, low mood, sleep problems or reduced function during structured history
May report tobacco exposure, inactivity, unhealthy diet or occupational risk
May have overdue vaccination or cancer screening
physicalSigns: Elevated or discrepant blood-pressure readings
Raised body-mass index or waist circumference
Oral-health, vision, hearing or mobility concerns
Abnormal findings requiring conversion from screening to a diagnostic pathway

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Asymptomatic, eligible by age or risk and suitable for a validated screening intervention.
Known diagnosis or repeated abnormal result requiring disease-specific targets rather than screening thresholds.
Symptoms or signs raise pre-test probability and require diagnostic, not screening, tests.
Single clinic value is not confirmed on repeat or out-of-office measurement.

ruleIn.testName: Standardised blood-pressure measurement with out-of-office confirmation
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standardised blood-pressure measurement with out-of-office confirmation — Hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Persistently elevated readings confirmed outside the clinic when indicated.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Reduces misclassification from technique, white-coat effect and isolated readings.

ruleIn.testName: Risk-based glucose testing
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Risk-based glucose testing — Prediabetes or diabetes
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Abnormal fasting glucose, random glucose in context or glycated haemoglobin confirmed through the diagnostic pathway.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: PHA guidance begins routine adult testing at the defined age and earlier with overweight plus risk factors.

ruleIn.testName: Age-, sex- and risk-appropriate cancer screening
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Age-, sex- and risk-appropriate cancer screening — Preclinical breast, colorectal, cervical or lung cancer
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Negative screening at the recommended interval or an abnormal result requiring timely diagnostic confirmation.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Preclinical breast, colorectal, cervical or lung cancer
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Benefit depends on eligibility, interval and complete follow-through after an abnormal screen.

ruleOut.testName: Repeat or confirmatory diagnostic test after an abnormal screen
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Repeat or confirmatory diagnostic test after an abnormal screen — False-positive screening result
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Diagnostic testing does not confirm disease.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Screening tests do not by themselves establish many diagnoses.

ruleOut.testName: Medication and comorbidity review
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Medication and comorbidity review — Secondary or iatrogenic risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A medicine, pregnancy state, renal disease or other condition explains or changes the preventive finding.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Prevents inappropriate application of general-population screening or treatment advice.

pathophysiology.summary: Periodic health examination is a risk-based preventive-care process rather than a disease episode. It identifies modifiable cardiovascular, metabolic, cancer, infectious, mental-health and functional risks before symptoms or irreversible complications develop, while avoiding screening that has an unfavourable balance of benefit and harm.
keyMechanisms: Age, sex, family history, exposures and comorbidity alter baseline disease probability and screening benefit.
Repeated measurement can detect trajectories in blood pressure, adiposity, glycaemia and lipids before complications emerge.
Evidence-based screening shifts selected cancers and chronic diseases toward earlier diagnosis.
Shared decisions reduce harms from false positives, overdiagnosis and preventive medicines with small net benefit.

clinicalManagement.title: Build an individual risk inventory
actions: Record age, sex, pregnancy potential, family history, tobacco exposure, occupation, medicines, comorbidity and prior screening.
Assess mental health, safety, function and social determinants with validated tools where appropriate.
Separate asymptomatic screening from symptoms that require diagnostic evaluation.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At each periodic examination

clinicalManagement.title: Complete core measurements
actions: Measure blood pressure using validated technique and assess body-mass index and waist circumference at the PHA interval.
Order glucose and lipid testing according to age and risk.
Review oral health, vaccination status and age-related vision, hearing, falls or cognition needs.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During the visit

clinicalManagement.title: Offer eligible screening
actions: Offer breast, cervical, colorectal, lung, osteoporosis and abdominal-aortic-aneurysm screening only when age, sex and risk criteria are met.
Explain likely benefits, limitations and follow-up before testing.
Create a closed-loop plan for every abnormal result.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At the guideline-defined interval

clinicalManagement.title: Deliver preventive interventions
actions: Provide indicated immunisation under the current Saudi schedule.
Offer tobacco-cessation treatment, physical-activity and dietary support.
Use generic preventive pharmacotherapy only after formal cardiovascular-risk, contraindication and shared-decision assessment.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At the same visit or scheduled follow-up

clinicalManagement.title: Close the preventive-care loop
actions: Communicate normal and abnormal results in understandable language.
Convert confirmed abnormalities to the relevant diagnostic or chronic-care pathway.
Update the recall date and assign ownership for referrals and pending tests.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After results are available

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Maintain a personalised recall schedule based on the 2023 PHA age and risk tables, review abnormal results promptly, and update eligibility whenever health status, family history, pregnancy status or exposure changes.
mdtReferrals: Primary-care nurse or preventive-care coordinator for recall and result tracking
Dietitian, tobacco-cessation service or exercise professional according to risk
Mental-health service for confirmed depression, anxiety or safety concern
Diagnostic specialty pathway for any abnormal screening result
lifestyleAndDiet: Support a sustainable dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains and minimally processed foods while accounting for culture and comorbidity.
Encourage regular aerobic and strengthening activity adapted to ability.
Provide tobacco cessation, sleep, weight and oral-health support without stigma.
patientEducation: Explain that preventive tests are selected by personal risk and that more testing is not always safer.
Use shared decision making for preference-sensitive cancer screening and preventive medicines.
Give accessible instructions for preparation, result access and the next step after an abnormal result.
dischargeCriteria: Risk profile, due interventions and deferred shared decisions are documented.
Every test and referral has a named owner and result-communication method.
Urgent symptoms or severe abnormalities have been diverted to immediate assessment.

redFlags: Severe allergic reaction history
Immunocompromise affecting live vaccines
Current acute illness or pregnancy influencing timing
Travel exposure with urgent prophylaxis window
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Adult Vaccination Review, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.

Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

Check registry or prior provider before deciding repeat schedule.

content.title: Acute Anaphylaxis
content.specialty: Emergency Medicine and Allergy and Immunology

redFlags: Airway swelling, stridor, severe bronchospasm or rapidly worsening breathing
Hypotension, syncope, confusion or shock
Refractory symptoms after intramuscular epinephrine
Known mast-cell disorder, severe asthma, beta-blocker use or prior biphasic/refractory anaphylaxis
symptoms: Sudden throat tightness, hoarse voice or difficulty swallowing
Breathlessness, wheeze or persistent cough
Generalised itching, flushing, urticaria or swelling
Dizziness, collapse, cramping abdominal pain or vomiting after a likely exposure
physicalSigns: Stridor, angioedema or respiratory distress
Wheeze, hypoxaemia or reduced air entry
Hypotension, tachycardia, poor perfusion or collapse
Generalised urticaria or flushing, noting that skin signs can be absent

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Predominantly lower-airway obstruction without hypotension, acute skin/mucosal change or a clear multisystem exposure response.
Bradycardia, pallor and rapid improvement supine without urticaria, wheeze or airway swelling.
Angioedema without urticaria, often slower onset and limited response to epinephrine or antihistamine.
Infective syndrome and less immediate exposure relationship, although initial shock management may overlap.

ruleIn.testName: Clinical diagnostic criteria
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Clinical diagnostic criteria — Anaphylaxis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Acute airway, breathing or circulatory compromise with compatible skin/mucosal findings or a likely allergen exposure.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis and treatment must not wait for laboratory confirmation.

ruleIn.testName: Serial serum tryptase when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serial serum tryptase when indicated — Systemic mast-cell activation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A rise above the person's baseline in an appropriately timed sample.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Can support later specialist evaluation but a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.

ruleOut.testName: Point-of-care glucose
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Point-of-care glucose — Hypoglycaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Glucose is not low enough to explain altered consciousness or collapse.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Rapidly excludes a reversible mimic while resuscitation continues.

ruleOut.testName: Electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrocardiogram — Primary arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No primary electrical or ischaemic cause for collapse.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Primary arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Particularly important in older patients, chest pain, severe hypotension or epinephrine-related symptoms.

pathophysiology.summary: Anaphylaxis is a rapid systemic hypersensitivity reaction. Mast-cell and basophil mediator release causes vasodilation, capillary leak, mucosal oedema and bronchoconstriction, which can progress quickly to airway obstruction, distributive shock and cardiac arrest.
keyMechanisms: IgE-mediated or non-IgE pathways trigger widespread mediator release.
Vasodilation and capillary permeability reduce venous return and blood pressure.
Upper-airway oedema and lower-airway bronchospasm compromise ventilation.
Biphasic recurrence can occur after apparent initial resolution.

clinicalManagement.title: Give intramuscular epinephrine
actions: Administer intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh using the current MOH age/weight dosing protocol.
Repeat at the protocol interval if airway, breathing or circulatory compromise persists.
Do not delay epinephrine for antihistamines, corticosteroids, intravenous access or diagnostic tests.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately

clinicalManagement.title: Position and support airway and breathing
actions: Lay the patient flat with legs elevated unless respiratory distress requires a supported position; avoid sudden standing or sitting.
Call the resuscitation team, give high-concentration oxygen when indicated and prepare early for a difficult airway.
Use inhaled bronchodilator as an adjunct for persistent bronchospasm, never as a substitute for epinephrine.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Concurrent with first epinephrine dose

clinicalManagement.title: Restore circulation
actions: Establish intravenous or intraosseous access and give rapid isotonic crystalloid with frequent reassessment.
Use continuous monitoring and obtain senior critical-care support for refractory shock.
Intravenous epinephrine infusion is restricted to appropriately monitored settings and experienced clinicians.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately when shock is present

clinicalManagement.title: Stop exposure and add adjunctive care
actions: Stop the suspected trigger when this can be done safely, such as halting an infusion.
After stabilisation, use adjunctive antihistamine for persistent skin symptoms according to local policy.
Do not rely on corticosteroids to prevent immediate deterioration or replace observation.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as feasible

clinicalManagement.title: Observe and plan safe discharge
actions: Use risk-stratified observation, extending monitoring after severe, refractory or high-risk reactions.
Document the suspected trigger and all treatment times.
Provide an emergency plan and allergy referral before discharge.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After complete clinical resolution

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange allergy evaluation, ensure the event is recorded in the medicine/allergy record, review auto-injector availability before expiry, and advise immediate emergency care for any recurrent systemic reaction.

patientEducation: Teach recognition of airway, breathing and circulatory symptoms and the need to use an epinephrine auto-injector without delay when prescribed.

Provide written trigger-avoidance and emergency instructions in the patient's preferred language.
dischargeCriteria: Airway, breathing, circulation and skin/mucosal symptoms have fully resolved for the risk-appropriate observation period.

Written precautions, suspected-trigger documentation and specialist follow-up are in place.

pathophysiology.summary: Atrial fibrillation is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia with disorganised atrial activation and ineffective atrial contraction. Irregular ventricular conduction can cause symptoms or tachycardia-mediated dysfunction, while atrial blood stasis promotes thrombus formation and systemic embolism.
keyMechanisms: Ectopic atrial triggers and a susceptible atrial substrate sustain chaotic electrical activation.
Loss of coordinated atrial contraction and irregular atrioventricular conduction reduce haemodynamic efficiency.
Blood stasis, endothelial dysfunction and prothrombotic factors increase left-atrial thrombus and stroke risk.
Hypertension, heart failure, valve disease, thyroid disease, obesity, sleep apnoea and alcohol can promote onset or recurrence.

pathophysiology.summary: Breast cancer comprises malignant epithelial tumours with heterogeneous hormone-receptor, HER2 and genomic biology. Disease may remain in situ, invade breast and regional lymphatics, or spread haematogenously to bone, liver, lung and brain; biology and stage jointly determine treatment and prognosis.
keyMechanisms: Accumulated genomic and epigenetic alterations enable uncontrolled proliferation and invasion.
Oestrogen/progesterone-receptor signalling and HER2 amplification define actionable biological subsets.
Lymphatic spread commonly involves axillary and regional nodes.
Tumour heterogeneity and treatment selection pressure can change receptor status in recurrent disease.

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, syncope with persistent hypotension or obstructive-shock features
Severe hypoxaemia, rapidly escalating oxygen requirement or cardiac arrest
Threatened limb with massive swelling, cyanosis or severe pain
Active major bleeding or another absolute barrier to anticoagulation in a patient with confirmed or highly suspected VTE
symptoms: Unilateral leg pain or swelling
Sudden unexplained dyspnoea
Pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis or syncope
Reduced exercise tolerance with recent immobility, surgery, cancer or prior thrombosis
physicalSigns: Unilateral pitting oedema, calf asymmetry or deep venous tenderness

Signs of right-heart strain such as raised jugular venous pressure

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Superficial erythema, warmth and a possible portal of entry with inflammatory features rather than isolated deep venous tenderness.
Posterior knee pathology with fluid tracking into the calf and diagnostic ultrasound findings.
Pressure-type pain, ischaemic electrocardiographic change or a coronary biomarker pattern rather than pleuritic pain and right-heart strain.
Focal infective symptoms or unilateral absent breath sounds with confirmatory chest imaging.

pathophysiology.summary: Venous thromboembolism results from venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. A deep-vein thrombus may obstruct limb venous return or embolise to pulmonary arteries, increasing dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance and, in severe cases, causing right-ventricular failure and shock.
keyMechanisms: Thrombus formation is promoted by immobility, surgery, cancer, oestrogen exposure, pregnancy and inherited or acquired thrombophilia.
Pulmonary arterial obstruction produces ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia.
Acute right-ventricular pressure overload can reduce left-ventricular filling and systemic cardiac output.
Residual venous obstruction and valve damage contribute to post-thrombotic syndrome; persistent vascular obstruction may cause chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

redFlags: Blood pressure at or above the severe range with retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema, confusion, chest pain, acute kidney injury or heart failure
Pregnancy or possible pregnancy with severe hypertension or concerning symptoms
Acute focal neurological deficit or aortic-dissection features
Suspected catecholamine crisis or another rapidly progressive secondary cause
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic and detected on screening
Headache or dizziness, which are non-specific
Symptoms of target-organ disease such as exertional chest discomfort, breathlessness or neurological episodes
Features suggesting a secondary cause, including episodic palpitations, muscle weakness or sleep apnoea
physicalSigns: Repeated elevated clinic blood pressure using correct technique
Postural blood-pressure fall in older adults, diabetes or symptomatic patients
Retinal vascular change
Signs of left-ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease or endocrine disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Raised clinic readings with normal validated ambulatory or home averages.
Normal clinic readings but elevated out-of-office averages or unexplained target-organ damage.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistant disease, hypokalaemia, renal findings, endocrine features or a medicine/substance trigger.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness or recent stimulant exposure with normal readings after the driver resolves.

ruleIn.testName: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure — Persistent clinic hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Clinic blood pressure remains at or above the diagnostic threshold after repeat measurement with correct cuff and positioning.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Technique and repetition reduce random error and identify inter-arm difference.

ruleIn.testName: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average waking readings meet the validated diagnostic threshold using adequate measurements.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Preferred confirmation method for clinic readings below the severe range and distinguishes white-coat effect.

ruleIn.testName: Home blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average readings after discarding the first day meet the validated home threshold.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides confirmation and supports later self-monitoring when performed with a validated device and protocol.

ruleOut.testName: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis — Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No albuminuria or haematuria, or an abnormality prompts renal evaluation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Renal disease can be both a cause and consequence of hypertension and changes treatment choice and targets.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile — Secondary contributor and cardiovascular comorbidity
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Baseline metabolic and renal status is defined; hypokalaemia, kidney dysfunction or diabetes redirects assessment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports cardiovascular-risk estimation and safe medicine selection.

ruleOut.testName: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram — Retinal or cardiac target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No hypertensive retinopathy or left-ventricular/cardiac abnormality, or damage is documented for risk management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Target-organ damage changes urgency and the balance of treatment benefit.

pathophysiology.summary: Sustained arterial hypertension reflects increased systemic vascular resistance, altered sodium-volume balance and neurohormonal activation interacting with age, genetics, adiposity and environmental exposures. Chronic pressure load accelerates vascular remodelling and damages the heart, brain, kidneys, retina and peripheral arteries.
keyMechanisms: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic activation increase vascular tone and sodium retention.
Endothelial dysfunction and arterial stiffness raise systolic pressure and pulse pressure.
Renal sodium handling and pressure natriuresis reset at a higher arterial pressure.
Persistent load causes left-ventricular hypertrophy, albuminuria, retinopathy and cerebrovascular injury.

lifestyleAndDiet: Reduce dietary sodium using culturally relevant food choices; avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes when kidney disease, diabetes or interacting medicines make them unsafe.

pathophysiology.summary: Lung cancer arises from malignant transformation of respiratory epithelium and is broadly classified as non-small-cell or small-cell carcinoma. Local invasion, lymphatic spread and early haematogenous dissemination determine resectability and systemic treatment; molecular drivers and immune phenotype increasingly guide therapy.
keyMechanisms: Tobacco smoke, environmental and occupational carcinogens produce cumulative genomic injury.
Histological subtype and molecular alterations determine growth pattern and treatment sensitivity.
Mediastinal nodal involvement strongly affects stage and curative options.
Metastatic spread commonly affects brain, bone, liver and adrenal glands; paraneoplastic syndromes may precede local symptoms.

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Endothelial injury, vasodilation, capillary leak, microvascular thrombosis and cellular metabolic dysfunction can impair tissue oxygen delivery and progress to shock and multiorgan failure.
keyMechanisms: An uncontrolled inflammatory and immune response disrupts endothelial integrity and vascular tone.
Relative and absolute hypovolaemia reduce effective circulating volume.
Microcirculatory dysfunction and coagulation activation impair organ perfusion.
Myocardial depression and cellular oxygen-utilisation defects can persist despite apparently corrected blood pressure.

content.title: Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

redFlags: Syncope, hypoxaemia, shock, or severe chest pain
Rapidly progressive swelling or suspected phlegmasia
Major bleeding or thrombocytopenia
Labour or planned neuraxial procedure while anticoagulated
symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Usually bilateral and gradual but does not exclude DVT.
Alternative causes of chest symptoms.
Peripartum collapse is distinct and immediately critical.
